I remember when I was your age, I was so focused on my career and trying to figure out my life. It took me a while to realize that family is what really matters.      I’ve been thinking about that a lot lately. I know I’m lucky to have you here, helping out with the baby and everything. It’s not the same as having a partner, but it’s close enough.      That’s the thing about family. We’re always there for each other, no matter what. Speaking of that, you mentioned earlier that you were going to be going to the weekend retreat with some of the other teachers. Are you going to be able to make it?      I think so. I’ll have to arrange some childcare, but I’m pretty sure my mum and dad are going to help out. They’ve been amazing.      That’s good. You should go. You deserve some time to yourself, even if it’s just for a day or two. It’s important to recharge.      I know. And I’ve also been thinking about signing with her. I’ve been taking those classes for a few weeks now, and I’m starting to feel more confident. It’s such a useful skill.      That’s great!

You know, I’ve always loved the countryside, but it’s only when you live here that you really start to appreciate the beauty of it. I mean, the rolling hills, the quiet villages—there’s something so peaceful about it all.      Yeah, I agree. There’s something about the silence here that makes you feel like you’re away from the noise of the city. I remember when I was a kid, my parents used to take me to the countryside for weekends. It was always such a contrast to the hectic life in London.      I can imagine. I’ve never lived in the city, but I definitely understand the appeal of the countryside. I mean, I grew up in Norwich, and even though it’s not exactly the middle of nowhere, it’s still got that charm. And when you come here, you just feel like you’re in a different world.      Speaking of which, I was thinking—do you know what it’s like to live in a village? Like, do you ever feel like you’re missing out on the action? I mean, I work in a university, so I’m used to being around people, but I sometimes miss the noise and the buzz of the city.      Honestly, I don’t think I would miss it. There’s a different kind of energy here. It’s not just about the quiet—it’s about the connection to nature. You can walk for miles and not see a soul, but when you do, it feels like a real community. Plus, the views are just incredible.      I guess you’re right. I mean, I have to admit, I do like the idea of living somewhere like this. It’s not that I don’t like London—I love it, don’t get me wrong—but there’s something about the countryside that feels more... grounded. Like you’re not just moving through life, but actually experiencing it.      Exactly. It’s not just about the landscape—it’s about the pace of life. You get to slow down, to think, to breathe. I think that’s why I’ve always felt drawn to this part of England. It’s like the land itself is telling you to take a moment and just be.      You know, I think I’m starting to understand that. It’s funny—being a lecturer, I often think about the world in terms of ideas and theories, but here, it’s all about experience and feeling.

So, I was just thinking about that film we watched last night,  The Banshees of Inisherin —it was so intense, wasn’t it? I mean, I didn’t expect that ending to hit me like that. It’s one of those movies that sticks with you for days.      Yeah, it definitely had that emotional weight. I mean, I love when films do that—make you feel something so deeply. But honestly, I couldn’t get the ending out of my head. It’s like, what if that’s how real life feels? Just… this quiet, unresolved tension?      Exactly. It’s like that one friend of mine, Sam, who’s got this job as a project manager. He’s always talking about how he’s “on the clock” and how he can’t just let things go. It’s like he’s constantly trying to fix everything, but sometimes you just need to let things be.      That’s funny, I was just thinking about Sam too. He told me he’s been working 12-hour days lately. He said he’s got this new project that’s taking over his life. I asked him if he was enjoying it, and he just said, “It’s a job, not a holiday.” You know, typical Sam.      Oh, he’s the kind of person who’d say that. But seriously, I feel for him. I mean, I’m in a different job, but I can see how it can weigh on you. I work in a corporate role, but I don’t have the same level of pressure. I mean, I’m not a consultant engineer, obviously.      Yeah, that’s a different world. I mean, I run my own projects, but I also have the freedom to be creative. I guess it’s a trade-off. I don’t have a boss breathing down my neck, but I do have deadlines and performance reviews. It’s not all glamour.      I get that. I guess we’re both in the professional world, just different sides of it. But hey, at least we can go out and ride our bikes on the weekends, right? I mean, I love cycling, especially when it’s just me and the wind.      Yeah, and there’s nothing like the feeling of freedom on a bike. Although, I did have this incident last week where a cyclist almost ran me over. I was driving, and he just came out of nowhere.

You know, I’ve always loved the way the flowers bloom here in Norfolk. It feels like the whole landscape is alive, especially in spring. I mean, the fields are just bursting with color.      Yeah, it’s incredible. I remember when we first moved here, I thought I’d never get used to the quiet. But now, I feel so at peace. It’s like the air here has a different rhythm. You can almost hear the earth breathing.      That’s true. I think it’s the combination of walking through these fields, the fresh air, and the fact that you’re not surrounded by the noise of the city. It’s the kind of place where you can really think.      I was thinking the other day about how different this is from London. Even though we both grew up in England, there’s something about the pace of life here that just feels more... grounded. I don’t know, maybe it’s the way the seasons move so clearly here.      It’s interesting how places shape you, isn’t it? I’ve written about that in my research. The socio-economic conditions of a place can influence people’s language, behaviors, even their perspectives on economics. For example, in some rural areas, people are more likely to rely on cash crops than in urban centers.      That’s a fascinating angle. I was thinking about how language evolves in different regions, and how even within England, there are subtle differences. I mean, just the way people pronounce words can change based on where you’re from.      Exactly. I’ve noticed that in my lectures, there’s a lot about how regional dialects are not just about the words people use, but about how they see the world. It’s almost like the language is a reflection of the land itself.      I couldn’t agree more. And speaking of land, did you know that some of the flowers here are actually indicators of the soil type? I read something about how certain flowers only grow in specific conditions. Like, if you see bluebells, you know the soil is more alkaline.      That’s brilliant. I think I need to do some research on that. It’s always amazing how nature has these little clues. Maybe I can write a paper on the symbiosis between agriculture and the local ecosystem.      That’s a great idea.

Right, so I’ve got this flat in Newcastle, and I need to get it ready for the move. But the problem is, I can’t find a parking spot near the flat. I’ve been trying to look online, but all the spots are either taken or too expensive.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I had that same issue when I moved to Cambridge. I ended up parking a few streets away and walking. It was a bit of a journey, but it was cheaper.      I can’t walk that far. I mean, I’ve got a car and I don’t want to leave it out in the open. I’m worried about it getting stolen or damaged.      You could check with the landlord or the estate agent. Maybe they know of some off-road parking options or something. Or maybe even a carport?      I did check with the agent, but they said the flat’s in a really busy area, so parking’s limited. I’m just hoping there’s some space in the building’s garage.      Did you ask about the garage? I’ve heard some places have underground car parks where you can park for a small fee.      I didn’t think of that. Maybe I should call them again and ask about that.      Yeah, that’s a good idea. Also, you could maybe check with the local council. They often have parking apps or websites where you can book spaces in advance.      I might do that. But I’m also thinking about the Angel of the North. I’ve always wanted to visit it. I heard the view from the car is amazing.      I know! The car park there is one of the best in the country. You can park for free and walk around. The views are worth it.      I might have to take a road trip up there. Maybe after I settle into the flat.      That’d be great. And speaking of trips, have you seen the Manchester derby?      Oh, I go every season. It’s a bit of a tradition now. I even got a season ticket last year.      You’re a real fan. I tried going once, but it was so packed and loud, I couldn’t even hear the team.      Yeah, it’s a bit like a rock concert. You’ve got to be ready for that.      I’ll take my chances.

Oh, I just saw an article about the celebrity trial—the one with that actor who got into a fight with his ex on a yacht. I can't believe it's already going to court again. You know, I’ve seen some wild things in my time, but that was something else.      Yeah, I remember hearing about that. It's so strange how people get into these ridiculous situations. But I guess fame has its perks, even if they’re not always positive. Speaking of strange things, have you seen the geese around the park lately?      Oh, I saw them yesterday. They were all gathered around the pond, like they were having a little meeting. I swear, they looked like they were arguing. I mean, they're just birds, right? But I swear, they had this intense look about them. Like they were planning something.      Oh, they’re not the only ones with drama, dear. I’ve seen them flying south for the winter, and I swear, it's like they're taking a pilgrimage. I remember when I was a kid, I used to follow them with my binoculars. It was like watching a whole army of little soldiers marching off to a new home.      That’s adorable. I’m sure they don’t know they’re being watched. I wonder if they ever get bored of the same routine. Like, do they ever try to go somewhere else? I mean, they’ve been here for years. Some of them must be thinking, “Why don’t we just take a break and go to Spain for a while?”      I can imagine that. But then again, they’re wild birds. They don’t have the luxury of a holiday. They’ve got to stick to the schedule, like clockwork. I mean, even if they’re not on a schedule, they still know it's time to fly when it gets cold.      Exactly. And you know what’s even more interesting? Some of the geese have little families with them. I’ve seen them carrying their babies on their backs, trying to keep them warm. It's heartwarming, really. I sometimes think they’re smarter than we give them credit for.      You know, I was just thinking the other day—if birds can migrate across the world, maybe humans could learn something from them. Like, maybe we don’t have to overcomplicate things.

So, I just wanted to say, I’m really impressed with how quickly you got the job at the new school. You were so nervous about the interview, weren’t you?      Oh, thank you! I was honestly terrified. I mean, I had a great interview, but I kept second-guessing my answers. I even got a bit shaky when the headteacher asked about my experience with younger children. I had never actually taught a baby before, but I tried to make it sound like I had.      Oh, come on! Didn’t you do that with your cousin’s baby last year? You were even helping with the feeding schedule and everything!      Yeah, I guess that’s what I was trying to reference. I just didn’t want to overstate it. I mean, I’m a teacher, not a babysitter. Although, I was definitely a bit of a babysitter, wasn’t I? I mean, I did take care of that little guy for hours when my cousin was working late.      That was amazing. I remember you were so calm and patient. You even managed to get him to smile when no one else could. It was like you had some kind of magic in your hands.      Oh, please! I just kept reminding myself that babies are just trying to figure out the world. I mean, the first time I picked him up, he just stared at me like I was some kind of alien. It was kind of funny. And then he started cooing at me after a while.      That’s the best part about babies, isn’t it? They’re so honest. No filters, no pretense. I think I miss that. I mean, I do teach, but it’s not the same as being around a baby all day. I think I need to have a baby of my own soon. My sister’s planning on having one next year. I can’t wait to experience that side of life again.      That sounds amazing. I hope you’re ready for the chaos. I mean, I had that one time when my cousin’s baby started screaming at 3 a.m., and I had to run over there just to get a cup of tea. I swear, I got more sleep in one day than I did in a week.      I’ll take that challenge. Although, maybe I should start with a little one.

So, I was just thinking about the future, you know? Like, what's going to happen in five years? I mean, I have this job now as a production controller, but I feel like I’m just doing the same thing every day. Sometimes I wonder if I’m on the right track.      Yeah, I get that. I’m in admin, which is pretty stable, but it’s not super exciting either. I mean, I’ve got a postgrad degree, so I guess I could be doing something more interesting. But I also don’t want to take a big risk. You know how it is, right?      Exactly. It’s like, do you go for the dream or do you play it safe? I’ve been thinking about going back to school. Maybe something in finance or business? I mean, if I’m going to run a business, I’d rather understand the ropes properly.      That’s smart. So, I’ve been meaning to ask—what exactly does a publishing assistant do, again? I’m still trying to wrap my head around the whole publishing process.      It’s not as glamorous as it sounds. We mostly deal with formatting manuscripts, proofreading, and coordinating with authors. It’s a mix of creativity and attention to detail.      Yeah, and we also handle the logistics—like getting the books ready for printing, making sure the files are clean, and coordinating with the printers. It’s like being a bridge between the author and the reader.      I think I still get confused sometimes. I’m not sure if I’m more of a temporary assistant or if I’m actually becoming part of the team. But I love the variety.      I can see why. You get to work with so many different projects and people. I mean, I’m a language research co-ordinator, so I spend most of my time analysing dialects and linguistic patterns. I don’t get to work as closely with the human side of publishing like you guys do.      You’re lucky, in a way. You can study people and how they speak, while we’re more like the hands-on people. I was born and raised in Aylesbury, so I’m used to the South-Eastern English dialect. I’ve done a lot of work on regional accents, especially in the UK.      I was born in England, but I’ve lived in a few different places. I think that gives me a bit of an ear for different dialects too.      I’m the odd one out here. I was born in Sweden, but I grew up in the UK. I speak English and Swedish, but I don’t really understand the English dialects as well as the rest of you. It’s kind of funny, because I’ve been in the UK for most of my life, and I still feel like I’m the outsider.      I know what you mean. Hey, mate, you’ve got the passport photo printed yet? I don’t know what’s gotten into me lately. I’ve been so tired all week, and I’m not even doing anything that hard. I feel like I’m running on empty.      You’re not the only one, honestly. I’ve been up all night writing essays, and now I’m just laying on the couch like a zombie. But I’ve been thinking about last night. Remember when we went to the hospital because you hurt your arm?      Oh yeah, that was crazy. I still can’t believe you called an ambulance for a dislocated shoulder. I mean, it was pretty bad, but I don’t think we needed to go to the ER.      I know, I know. I was just so panicked. I thought I was going to be stuck like that for days. And the doctor said it was just a minor dislocation, but it still took forever to pop back in.      And then we ended up staying at the hospital for hours, just chilling and eating pizza. I think that’s the only time I’ve ever seen you laugh so hard. You were practically crying.      I wasn’t crying, I was just… overwhelmed. I mean, it was funny, but I was also really scared. Maybe you’re just overworked. I mean, we’re all juggling so much—lectures, assignments, trying to find time to hang out. Maybe we’re all just burning out. Well, that was a proper do, wasn’t it? I thought I’d be the only one left standing by the end, but no, there was still a full house.      Yeah, it was mad. I mean, I didn’t think my aunt would actually bring that giant cake with the candles all the way from Manchester. I nearly got stuck in the door trying to get it in.      Oh, I remember that! You were squishing the cake like it was a football. And don’t even get me started on the debate about whether it was a birthday cake or a wedding cake.      I was just trying to be helpful, and I think I turned the whole room into a scene from a comedy show. Wait, did you actually say that the cake was for the 50th anniversary?      Yeah, that’s why it was so big—nearly three feet tall. I think it cost more than the actual party. But it was worth it. I mean, seeing all those faces, hearing the old songs, it brought back a lot of memories.      Yeah, it was good. I didn’t realize how many people still remembered the old days. I mean, my cousin Liam—he even made a joke about how he used to chase you around the garden with a bucket of water when you were a kid.      Oh, that’s one I still remember! You were so reckless, trying to get me with that bucket. And you nearly drowned the cat too. I still haven’t forgiven you for that.      Well, I was just trying to make you smarter. You always got confused with your sums, and I thought a bit of water would help.      You were a menace. But you did grow up. You’re doing well at school, aren’t you?      Yeah, I’m getting into it. I’m on the Science and Maths course now, and it’s actually pretty cool.      That’s good. You know, I used to be a maths examiner. I’ve seen plenty of students struggle with the same things you are. It’s not easy, but you’ve got the head for it.      Thanks. I guess I just like solving problems. My teacher says I’m pretty good at it.      It’s not just about the numbers, you know. It’s about understanding the world. And I think you’re on the right path.

You know, Dad, I’ve been thinking—do you remember when we first moved to Bolton? I was about eight, and I used to get so excited about the new house. It had this amazing cat flap that only the cat could use! I used to try to squeeze through it, and every time, I’d end up stuck with my little backpack on.      Oh, I remember that! You were so determined to be a cat. I used to have to rescue you from the garden. You’d be outside, covered in grass, and your backpack would be full of toys. I’d have to grab you and bring you back in, and you’d be like, “I’m not a dog, I’m a cat!”      Yeah, and then I started school. Remember how I used to bring my water bottle to class? I called it my “magic cup” because I thought it could make me smarter. And I always had to keep it full, or else the examiners would think I was cheating.      You were always dramatic. But honestly, that bottle was your lifeline. You’d refill it every time you went to the canteen. I think you even tried to bottle the lunch lady’s soup once.      Yeah, and don’t even get me started on the time I tried to mail a chocolate bar to my friend in Bolton. I thought it would be a gift, but it got lost. I had to wait a week for it to come back with a note that said, “It’s been inspected by the post office.”      That’s gold. You were always into the little things. Speaking of little things, have you thought about what you want to do when we get to Cornwall? I heard there’s a farm nearby with chickens and sheep. Maybe we can visit?      Yes! I’d love to see the animals. And I’ve been meaning to ask you about that time you had to move out of your old house. You said the washing machine broke the day you left. How’d you manage?      Oh, that was a disaster. I had to borrow a machine from a neighbor, and it was so loud I thought the house was haunted. You were already in bed by then. I just kept telling myself, “It’s just a washing machine.”      I can only imagine. You’re the type to make everything sound dramatic.

So, I was sorting through old boxes in the attic this morning, and I found this letter from my grandmother—written in the 1950s, mind you. It's all in that lovely, cursive handwriting, and it’s about her days as a headmistress at a school in Edinburgh. I mean, I didn’t even know she had that job.      That’s interesting. I’ve heard stories about her being quite strict, but I never thought she had such a role. I mean, when I was growing up, she was just the matriarch of the family—always cooking, always knitting, always worrying about us. But she had that career too?      Oh, I remember her well. She was the headmistress of a school in Glasgow for most of her life. She was very respected. She often spoke about the challenges of managing a staff and keeping the students on track. She always said that discipline was key, but she was also very kind to the children who struggled.      She really had a way with people. I’ve read some of the letters she wrote to her colleagues, and they were full of passion. I was just wondering if she ever thought about what it meant to be a headmistress in the 1950s—especially in Scotland.      Oh, she did. She often said that being a headmistress in Scotland was different from being one in England. There was a stronger sense of community, and the expectations were different too. She had to be more hands-on, more involved in the lives of the students and their families.      I can imagine. I’ve always found it fascinating how people’s roles and responsibilities change over time. My job as an administrator is quite different from hers, but I do sometimes think about the kind of leadership she must have had. I mean, she was managing an entire school, not just a department.      Hey, I heard the conversation about the headmistress. That's interesting. I’ve worked with headteachers before, and I can tell you, it’s not an easy job. You have to manage people, budgets, and expectations all at once. But from what I hear, your grandmother must have had a lot of respect.      She did. I always thought she was a bit of a legend, even in her own family. It’s amazing how someone can go from being a headmistress to being the matriarch of the family, right?

Okay, I think I’ve got everything sorted for Mother’s Day. The kids are excited to go to Forest School today, and I’ve already booked a few things for the weekend. Let me just check with them.      Can we go to the park, Mummy? I want to see the ducks.      Of course you can, sweetheart. But today’s Forest School is going to be a bit different. We’re going to do some activities that are more about nature and learning, not just playing. You’ll get to make things with sticks and leaves.      What do we make? Can we make a monster?      That’s a good idea, but maybe we’ll stick to something more eco-friendly. Maybe a birdhouse or a leaf crown. I think it’s going to be a great day.      I like leaf crowns. Can I wear a flower one?      That sounds lovely. I can make you one. But first, let’s make sure we’ve got everything ready for Forest School. I’ve got a bag with all the materials. Oh, and I found a new joke I want to tell you both.      What’s the joke?      Why don’t skeletons fight each other? Because they don’t have the guts!      That’s silly! I don’t like skeletons.      Me neither, but they’re funny in their own way. Speaking of funny, I remember this one from when I was your age. It’s about a chicken and a cow. The chicken crossed the road to get to the other side. The cow said, “Why did you cross the road?” The chicken said, “To get to the other side!” Then the cow said, “I’m going too.” And then they both crossed the road.      Why did the cow do that? Was it because of the chicken?      That’s the thing about idioms, love. Not everything makes sense at first, but that’s part of the fun. Like "cross the road" isn’t just about walking from one side to the other—it’s about making a decision or taking a step toward something.      So, the cow was making a decision?      Exactly. And that’s what Mother’s Day is about too—making decisions that show love and care for the people we’re close to.      So, is Mother’s Day a decision?      It’s more than that. It’s a celebration. But I think you’ll both love the Forest School today.

So, I just got a call from the doctor, and it’s not good news. They think my mum’s got cancer again. I mean, she’s had it before, and we were all hoping it was in remission. But apparently, they found something in her lungs.      Oh no, that’s terrible. I’m so sorry to hear that. How is she feeling? Has she been in hospital yet?      She’s been feeling really unwell for a while now—just tired, losing weight, coughing a lot. We thought it was just the cold or something, but now it’s confirmed. She’s in the hospital for tests and scans, and they’re trying to figure out what stage it’s at.      That’s really worrying. I can’t imagine how hard this must be for you. You know, my dad was diagnosed with lung cancer a few years back. He had surgery, chemo, and radiation. It was a long, hard battle. But he fought hard, and he was in great spirits until the end.      I know, and I hope she’s strong like that. But it’s still so early days, and I’m not sure how much time we have. I’m trying to be strong for her, but honestly, it’s exhausting. I feel like I’m constantly worrying about what’s next.      I can only imagine. It must be so hard to see someone you love going through this. Have you talked to the rest of the family about it? I mean, it’s not just you who has to deal with this.      We’ve had a few family meetings, but it’s still so hard to talk about. My brother’s still overseas, and my sister’s been really emotional. I think it’s easier to be strong when you’re alone, but I don’t know if that’s the right way to be.      I think you’re doing the right thing by being there for her. You don’t have to be strong all the time. It’s okay to feel overwhelmed. I remember when my dad was ill, I used to think I had to be the rock, but in reality, I just needed to be there, to listen, to hold her hand.      You’re right. I just wish I could do more. I mean, I can’t make the cancer go away, but I want to make sure she knows how much she means to me.

Hey, thanks for coming over today. You know, I’ve been thinking a lot about university lately. I mean, I’m not sure if I’m ready to fully commit to a research project yet. It's all so overwhelming. Do you ever feel like you're being pulled in a million directions?      I totally get that. I’ve been struggling with my timetabling too. It’s like I have to balance all these different modules, and then there's the whole thing with tuition fees. I know you mentioned you’re teaching English, so how do you manage working with students while still studying?      It’s not easy. I’ve had to juggle classes, grading, and my own research. But honestly, I love it. There's something about being able to help others learn the language I’m so passionate about. It keeps me motivated. Speaking of teaching, did you ever consider becoming an English teacher? I mean, your grasp of the language is pretty solid.      Honestly, I thought about it, but I’m still figuring out what I want to do long-term. I guess I’m more into linguistics—specifically how languages shape our thoughts. Did you ever think about that? Like, how different dialects or even accents affect how people perceive each other?      Definitely. I often think about how people judge others based on how they speak. I mean, I grew up in Bedford and have a pretty standard accent, but I know that in cities like London, people have such diverse accents. It’s fascinating. I wonder how that plays into how people are treated socially.      It does. I’ve noticed that in South Korea, for instance, there’s a huge focus on conformity, even in the way people speak. I read this article about how they use language to reinforce social hierarchies. It’s a bit scary, honestly. Maybe that’s why I’m so interested in how language affects identity.      That’s really interesting. I’ve been thinking about studying abroad too. Maybe I’ll go to China or South Korea. I’ve always wanted to immerse myself in a different culture. Do you think you’d ever consider studying abroad?      I’m actually looking into a program in Seoul next year. I’ve been fascinated by their festivals and how food plays such a big role in their culture. I’d love to explore food combinations there, especially since I’m a vegetarian.

So, I just got back from Sugarhouse last night. It was  so  chaotic. I mean, I saw Jack Whitehall there—actually, I think it was his brother, but I’m not sure. Either way, I got very close to a group of people who were all dressed like the characters from  The Vampire Diaries . It was like a cross between a nightclub and a Halloween party.      Oh, I saw that too! I was like, “Is that  actually  a real person?” But then, when they started dancing to  Twilight  soundtrack covers, I just knew it was a real party.      Yeah, I’ve seen enough of those. I tried to go to Sugarhouse once, but I got stuck in the queue for the bathroom for 45 minutes. And when I finally got in, the only thing I saw was a guy in a  Harry Potter  shirt.      That sounds like my night. I was there with my friends, and we got stuck in a line for three hours just to get a drink. I ended up drinking flavoured vodka out of a bottle like it was a lemonade.      I got a gift card for  The Big Fat Quiz  because of Secret Santa. It was so bad. I couldn’t even finish it.      Oh no, did you get the book? Or the DVD? Because I got a  Chaos Walking  trilogy for Christmas, and I thought it was a movie. I ended up reading it in bed and nearly fell asleep.      I got a box of cooking supplies. I tried to make pizza, but I burnt the dough. My flatmates had to do the rest.      Yeah, I got a set of sports kit tops. I was like, “Oh, this is perfect for when I go out with the boys.” Then I realized they were all white and had no sleeves.      Okay, but you  did  get the best present. The one that was goody bag with snacks and a mini bottle of wine.      That’s the one. I still have that bottle. It’s been in my drawer for 3 months and I haven’t opened it.      Speaking of presents, I bought a box of chocolates for my flatmate, and I put them in a jar. Then I forgot it was there until two weeks later. I opened it and saw that the chocolates had gone completely moldy.      That’s like when I tried to give my friend a plant for her birthday, and it died in two days.

So, I was just thinking about that time we tried to get the car started on that road trip. You remember? That one time in the Lake District when we were trying to get to Keswick and the engine just wouldn’t turn over.      Oh, I remember  everything  about that trip. You tried to jump-start it with that old battery from the van, and it just sparked like a fireworks show.      Yeah, and you said it was the “world’s most dramatic way to start a car.” I still think that’s the most vivid memory of that whole trip.      I know, right? It was like a comedy of errors. You were trying to talk to the guy in the van, and he was trying to fix the alternator, and then the car just started with a  pop  and we were off.      It’s funny how those little mishaps turn into such good stories. I mean, even though we were stuck in the middle of nowhere for like an hour, it turned into one of our favorite road trip memories.      Definitely. It’s the kind of thing that you’d never plan on, but it ends up being the highlight. You ever think about how those random moments often end up being the ones that stick with you the most?      Always. I think it’s because they’re so unexpected. When you’re in the middle of something planned, like a holiday or a trip, the unplanned stuff becomes the highlight.      Exactly. So, I guess that’s why we always end up talking about those moments when we’re about to fall asleep. You know, the ones where the car starts, the vibes are right, and you just feel like everything is perfect.      Maybe that’s the secret to life, though—embracing the chaos. I mean, if we had just gone straight to the hotel and ordered takeout, we’d never have that story.      True. I think that’s what makes us so good at our jobs, too. Like, I’ve got this engineering degree, but you’ve got this amazing ability to turn a disaster into a story.      Oh, don’t get me started. I’m the one who always ends up telling the stories. You’re just the guy who fixes the cars.      That’s what I’m here for. You tell the stories, I fix the problems.

You know, I’ve been feeling a bit off lately. Not sure if it’s the cold or just getting older, but I’ve been getting these strange pains in my back. I don’t think it’s anything serious, but I’m just worried.      I’ve been feeling that way too. I think it’s the weather, honestly. This constant dampness in the air just gets to you after a while. And don’t get me started on the wind—it’s like it’s trying to blow us all away.      I’ve been noticing that too. I’ve been feeling more tired than usual, even though I’m not doing anything heavy. I’m not sure if it’s the lack of exercise or if I’ve just been under a lot of stress lately. I’ve been working on some research for my lecture series, and it’s been taking a toll.      I hear you. I’ve been working late into the night so much that I’m practically a zombie by the time I get home. But I can’t complain too much—good work pays off, right? Although I’ve started to wonder if we’ve been too focused on work and not enough on our health.      I agree, but sometimes it feels like there’s not much time. Especially with the weather being so unpredictable. You know what I mean? One minute it’s sunny, the next it’s pouring with rain. It’s making it hard to get out and about.      And then there’s the football—can you believe the state of the pitch at the local ground? It’s like a swamp. I tried to take the kids to watch a game last week, and they almost fell into the puddles. I’m telling you, the weather has to be getting to them.      I’m sure the pitch is the least of their worries. Do you know how many times I’ve had to explain to students that the weather is as important as the curriculum? It’s always a topic of conversation.      Exactly. And let’s not forget the gadgets. I’ve been looking into buying a new laptop for work, but I’m not sure which one to go for. There are so many options out there, and I keep getting caught up in the specs. It’s like trying to figure out how to read a football match.

Hey, girls! It’s been way too long. How have you all been? I feel like we haven’t caught up in ages.      Oh my goodness, I know! It’s been like months. I’ve been so busy with work and trying to plan my sister’s wedding. It’s a total whirlwind, honestly.      I can only imagine. Is it in the same town? I mean, if it’s in Peterborough, maybe we can all make it?      Actually, no, it’s in London. But it’s such a big event. I’ve been juggling meetings, coordinating with vendors, and trying to keep the décor on track. Honestly, I’m exhausted.      I’m so sorry you’re going through that. I had my cousin’s wedding last year and I felt the same way. It’s one thing to plan something for yourself, but when it’s for someone else, it feels like you’re running a whole business.      That’s true. I can’t even imagine planning a wedding. I mean, I’ve never been into the whole "marriage and kids" thing, but I do respect people who want that. It just seems so overwhelming.      I think it’s just the whole "expectations" part. Like, you’re not just planning the event, you’re planning a future. It’s not just about the day itself, it’s about the whole package.      Exactly. And then there’s also the pressure from family and friends. I feel like everyone has an opinion on who you should marry, or how you should be raising your kids. It’s so much more than just a party, you know?      I know, it’s like the whole "modern woman" thing. You know, the idea that women should have it all—career, family, and a perfect life. But it’s not always possible. I mean, I just got promoted at work, and I’m still figuring out how to balance that with social life.      That’s exactly what I’m going through. I always thought I’d be a "traditional" woman with a husband and kids, but lately, I’m questioning that. I mean, I still want to have a family, but I also don’t want to give up my independence.      I completely get that. I think it’s a lot to navigate. I have a few friends who are in the same boat. Some are married, some are not, and some are just figuring it out.

You know, I’ve been trying to get my head around this new tablet thing. I’ve got one now, but I still don’t know how to use half the buttons. I keep pressing things by accident and the screen just goes blank. It’s like it’s trying to laugh at me.      I remember when I first got a mobile phone. I thought it was just a glorified calculator. Now I can’t even remember what a phone is without a camera and a screen. It’s like the whole world’s changed.      I couldn’t believe it when I got my first laptop, back when I was in teaching. My students thought it was magic. Now I can’t believe I used to write essays on paper. I still can’t get my head around the email thing. It feels like a letter, but it goes through the air and doesn’t need a postman.      I remember when we used to send letters to each other. I used to write to my mum in Norfolk every week. Now, I just send a text and she gets it in minutes. It’s quick, but I miss the feeling of holding a letter in my hands. Doesn’t feel quite right, somehow.      I know what you mean. I still write to my daughter every now and then, but she’s always asking me to send her photos instead. She’s got a phone now, so she never reads a letter. It’s like the old ways are fading away.      I think it’s just the way things go. You adapt, or you get left behind. I used to teach kids how to use computers, but now they’re all used to having touch screens and apps. It’s like a whole new world.      I suppose I have to keep up, but I don’t like the way it’s all so fast. I used to work with horses and it was all about patience. You can’t rush a horse, and you can’t rush a child either. I think that’s why I’m so slow with technology. It’s not about speed, it’s about knowing when to do things.      You’re right. I think the kids these days go so fast, they forget about patience. I used to play games with my grandkids, like chess or checkers.

You know, I’ve been thinking a lot about language lately. It’s such a big part of who we are, isn’t it? I teach it every day, and it’s amazing how it can bring people together—or sometimes divide them.      I can’t argue with that. I’ve always said that language is like a key. You can unlock a lot with the right words. Though I must say, I’ve never been one for pulling out a dictionary. My days were spent in boardrooms, not in books.      That’s funny. I used to work in finance before I became a teacher, but I always had a soft spot for languages. I suppose it’s because I grew up in Hitchin, where everyone seems to speak with a slight accent, and I used to think I was the only one who didn’t. It took me a while to realize that’s just how it is.      Oh, I know what you mean. I was born in Essex, and I used to feel that way too. My accent, I mean. I remember when I first started working in London, I was told I had a “distinctive” way of speaking. I thought it was a compliment until I realized it meant no one else spoke like that.      That’s the thing about accents. They can be such a part of your identity. I find it fascinating how people from the same region can sound so different. I mean, I teach both British and international students, and it’s always interesting to hear how they adapt their speech to fit in.      I suppose that’s the thing about living in a city like Birmingham. You’re always surrounded by different accents, different dialects. I used to love that. It made the city feel alive. I used to take long walks just to hear people talk—every corner, every street, had its own sound.      That’s a great way to learn. I think I’ll try that. I’ve been meaning to explore more of Birmingham anyway. I’ve been planning a weekend trip to the city centre. Do you want to come?      I’d love to. It’s been a while since we’ve done anything like that. Though I have to say, I’m not sure I’ll be able to keep up with all the new slang. I’ve been retired for a while, and I’ve lost touch with the youth.

So, I just got back from my weekend trip with my boyfriend. I was supposed to spend Valentine’s Day with him, but it ended up being a disaster.      Oh no, what happened? I thought you two were finally getting somewhere.      Yeah, we were, but then he  accidentally  told me he had a date with his ex on Saturday night. I mean, I knew it wasn’t over, but I got really hurt.      That sounds really frustrating. Did you confront him?      I did. I was like, “Are you even  trying ?” And he said he was just being friendly.      Ugh, that’s so frustrating. I’ve been through that. I had a guy who would text me “see you later” and then message his ex in the same conversation.      Exactly! I just feel like no matter how much I try to make it work, he’s not putting in the effort.      I get it. I mean, you deserve someone who’s actually into you. But maybe you should just focus on your own thing for now. Like, maybe go out with friends or do something fun this weekend.      Yeah, I’m thinking about going to the cinema with my roommate tonight. We’re seeing  The Marvels —I heard it’s really good.      Oh, I love Marvel. I’m gonna go with you. That way, I can just forget about my problems for a while. Also, I’ve been meaning to try that new restaurant near the university. The one with the chicken tikka masala.      Oh, that’s the one! I’ve heard it’s amazing. I’ll meet you there after the movie.      Perfect. But first, let’s go grab some food before the movie. I’m starving.      You’re always starving.      You know me. I’m from the Midlands, I’m used to eating every two hours.      Well, I’m from London, so I’m used to surviving on toast and coffee.      You’re lucky you’ve got a roommate who knows how to cook.      Yeah, she’s the only reason I can still function. So, what about you? Are you going out this weekend?      I was thinking of going shopping. I need new clothes for the summer.      You’re so into fashion. I can’t even tell what you’re wearing half the time.      Hey, I have  style . You just don’t know how to look.      Says the girl who can’t find her own socks half the time.

So, I just got my first major project approved — a sustainable housing development in East London. It’s going to be a mix of social housing and private apartments, and I’m really excited about the potential impact it could have on the local community. But honestly, it’s been a bit of a nightmare dealing with the council and the developers. I feel like the system is just so broken.      Oh no, that sounds like a lot of work. I can’t even imagine trying to navigate the housing system here. I mean, I rent a small flat in Kensal Rise, and I still feel like I’m being treated like a second-class citizen just because I don’t own property. It’s not just about money — it’s about power, right? The people who control the housing market have so much influence.      Exactly. And I think it’s tied up with the bigger picture — like capitalism and how it doesn’t really serve ordinary people. I mean, I grew up in Watford, and I remember how the housing prices went through the roof in the last decade. My parents had to move out of their own home because it became too expensive to maintain. It’s not just about supply and demand anymore — it’s about greed.      I completely agree. And then there’s the political angle — the government’s been so silent on the issue, even though it’s huge. I mean, there’s all this talk about equality and diversity, but when it comes to housing, the reality is that people of color and lower-income communities are the ones getting the short end of the stick.      Yeah, and it’s not just about race. It’s also about class. Look, I’m in a higher professional occupation, and even I’m struggling to afford a decent home. I mean, I can’t even buy a house in London, let alone afford the rent. It’s so frustrating to see how the system is designed to keep people like us in limbo.      I know. It’s exhausting being part of the system and feeling like you’re constantly fighting against it. But you know, I’m writing an article about this right now. I’m trying to highlight the intersection between housing, capitalism, and racial inequality. I think it’s important to make the connection clear — because so many people don’t realize how interconnected these issues are.

You know, I’ve been thinking a lot about the nursery lately. It’s only a few weeks away, and I still don’t feel fully ready.      I know, I can totally relate. I keep imagining how it’s going to go—what if the baby cries all the time? What if the other kids are too loud? I feel like I’m not prepared for anything.      You’re not alone in that. I remember when I first started thinking about going back to work, I had the same worries. But you just have to take it one day at a time.      I guess. I just worry about how I’ll manage everything—work, the baby, and then the holidays. I don’t even know if I’ll be able to take a proper break.      You don’t have to do it all on your own. You’ve got me, and I’m sure your mum will help too. And you know, once you get into the rhythm of things, it’ll feel more manageable.      I hope so. I was also thinking about the weening—how it’s going to feel, you know? Like, when will I finally be able to sleep through the night again?      Oh, I remember that. It felt like a miracle when I first got a full night’s sleep. But it’s all part of the journey. You’ll get through it.      I guess. I just hope I’m not making the same mistakes as my mum did. I mean, she had no idea about anything when she started.      Well, she found her way through, didn’t she? And you’re going to be just fine. You’ve got a lot of support, and you’ve got the strength to handle it.      I hope so. I also want to plan a little holiday soon—maybe somewhere warm? Like the coast?      That sounds perfect! I think it would do us both good to get out of the house for a while. You need a break, and the baby needs fresh air and sunshine.      Yeah, I think that’s a good idea. It’ll help me feel more like myself again.      You’ll be back to your old self in no time. And when you do, we can catch up on all the TV shows you’ve been missing. I’ve been binge-watching some old dramas.      I’ve been avoiding them, honestly.

Well, I can’t believe it’s already Friday. I feel like we’ve had a full week, but somehow it’s gone by so fast. How are you all holding up?      I’m surviving, mostly. Work’s been a bit of a nightmare this week, honestly. I got pulled into a meeting that stretched for hours, and then I had to sit through a report on how we’re underperforming in the charity sector. It was exhausting.      That sounds familiar. I’ve been dealing with the same thing at the store. One day, I’m managing a team, the next, I’m handling a customer complaint that turns into a full-blown argument. I think I’ve lost more hair this week than I did in the entire last year.      You’ve got to be kidding. I’ve been working late this week, trying to get the new marketing campaign up to the client’s standards. They’re not happy with the budget, and I’m under pressure to deliver something that doesn’t break the bank. Honestly, I’m tired of the constant back-and-forth.      I can imagine. You work in a high-pressure environment, so it’s no wonder you’re stressed. I, on the other hand, have been dealing with something else entirely. I got a call from the police today. They wanted a statement about that incident at the shop last week.      Oh no, did something happen?      Not really. It was just a minor thing – someone accused me of not being on the premises at the time of the break-in. But I had proof from my phone bill. Wait, maybe I should have mentioned that earlier. I have this EE phone bill that came in with a text from the police asking for my location.      Wait, was that the same time as the break-in? I thought you said your phone was lost.      No, I didn’t lose my phone. I just let it drop in the shower the other day and had to replace it. That’s why I have this new one. So I guess the police think I might have been in the area, but I can prove I was at home. It’s a bit of a hassle, honestly.      I can see how that would be frustrating. But at least you have proof. I wish I had that kind of evidence.

Hey man, it's great to see you again! How's everything going since your wedding? I heard it was a big event.      Oh, it was a doozy! A proper feast, loads of guests, and my mum was like a fairy godmother—well, more like a real one, if you know what I mean. But honestly, I think I'm still in shock that I'm married. A real life partner, not just a project or a phase.      That's huge. You've come a long way from when we first met, arguing over whether  Spartacus  was more of a TV show or a historical drama.      Yeah, I still think that one’s a bit of both. The fighting is good, but the costumes? They look like they're from the 1930s. But hey, I’m not complaining. I’ve been binge-watching it again lately. It’s like a time machine to ancient Rome, even if it's a little inaccurate.      I’ll give you that. I mean, the Romans, the Spartans, the whole idea of warriors and empires—it’s like a Netflix documentary series for history nerds like us. Speaking of which, have you seen the new series about the fall of the Roman Empire? It’s pretty intense, and I think they even used some real historical figures.      I’ve heard about it, but I’m not sure I can handle the drama. I mean, people dying early? That’s not my thing. It just feels like a cruel twist of fate. Like, why would the gods want to punish their own?      Oh, come on, we all know it’s just the show’s way of keeping us watching. But I can’t help but think about how some of these historical figures were really ahead of their time. You know, like using herbs for medicine, or even something like nuts and chickpeas. I mean, they were smart people.      Yeah, I guess you’re right. I’ve been thinking about starting a small herb garden in the back of the flat. Maybe even a little mortar and pestle for grinding spices. I’ve always been curious about the way different cultures use herbs and spices in their cooking.      That sounds cool. I’ve been into that too, especially since I teach English. You know, sometimes I’ll bring in recipes from different countries and talk about the history behind the ingredients.

Hey, have you seen the new poster for the school orchestra? I think it's in the music room. I got it from Mrs. Harper this morning.      Oh, you mean the wind-band thing? Yeah, I saw it! I was walking past the music room and it was all bright and colorful. Are you going to try out?      I’m actually thinking about it. I’ve never played any instrument before, but I’ve always loved listening to music. It’d be fun to try. What about you?      Me? I don’t know. I’ve never been very good with instruments, honestly. I mean, I can play the keyboard a little, but I’m not sure if I’d be good enough. Plus, I’m not sure if I have the time.      I think it’s worth a try. You never know, you might surprise yourself. What do you think about the English test coming up?      Ugh, I’m not looking forward to it. I got 58% on the last one, and I feel like I’m not improving. I’m so stressed about it.      I know, it’s been a bit rough. But maybe we can study together? I got a few notes from the teacher about the new grammar points, and I could help you go through them.      That would be great! I was thinking the same thing. We could meet after class today. Oh, and did you get the French lesson schedule from Miss Walker?      Yeah, I did. It’s a bit hectic, but it’s good to know where we’re going. I’m actually excited about the art lessons this week. We’re doing a painting project, and I’m really looking forward to it.      Me too! I love art, even though I’m not the best at it. I mean, I can draw okay, but I’m more into painting. I think I’m going to try some watercolors this week.      That sounds cool. I might try that too. It’s always nice to have a break from the English and French stuff, even if it’s just for a class.      Yeah, totally. I think it’s important to have a balance. School can get really intense sometimes, especially with all the tests and projects.      Definitely. I mean, I’m feeling the pressure, but I’m trying to stay positive. I think if we all work together, we can make it through.

You know, I still can’t get over how different the accents are in this part of the country. It’s like every town has its own dialect. I swear, sometimes I can’t understand my own family when they come from Newcastle.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I grew up in Newcastle, and even though I’ve been living in Darlington for a few years now, sometimes I still slip into that Yorkshire lilt. My mum still calls me “laddie” when she’s annoyed, and I don’t know why I let her get away with it.      That’s the thing about accents, isn’t it? They’re like a badge of identity. I used to teach English, and I’d always tell my students that accents aren’t just about how you speak—they tell you where you’re from, what you’ve been through, and even how you see the world. I still hear it in my head, even though I’ve been out of teaching for a while.      That’s true. I’ve always thought about that. Especially now, as I work in administration. You can tell a lot about someone just by how they speak. I remember when I was teaching, I used to have a student from Liverpool who, despite being barely 16, had the most articulate way of speaking. It was impressive.      And I’ve got a cousin who speaks with an accent so strong, even my mum can’t understand him half the time. He’s from the Yorkshire Dales, and he’s got this way of using “wot” and “y’know” everywhere. I think he’s trying to sound more “local,” but honestly, he just sounds confused.      That’s classic. I used to joke that if you put someone from Nottingham and someone from Liverpool in a room, they’d have a conversation in a dialect that no one can understand. I tried once, just for laughs, and I swear my students thought I was putting on a play.      That would’ve been a class act. I still remember one of my students who started using the word “bloody” in every sentence. I had to ask him why he was so obsessed with it, and he just said, “It’s British, Miss.” I didn’t know what to say.      I think I’ll take that as a compliment. I mean, “bloody” is like the national sport of the UK.

So, I was driving back from Cambridge yesterday and had to swerve to avoid a... well, let's just say it was a very  animated  cyclist. I think he might have been doing a bit of moonlighting, or maybe he just needed a break from his job.      You mean he was doing a bit of "jig saw" work on the road? I once had a customer who thought he was building a puzzle while riding a bike. Ended up crashing into a lamppost. Didn’t even get a ticket, just a lecture from the council.      I know, I know. My neighbor’s son used to do that. He’d ride his bike with a jigsaw in his hand, like he was trying to build something. The poor man got a fine for dangerous driving.      I think it’s more about the genes, though. I’ve got this cousin who’s obsessed with jigsaws—and I mean  obsessed . He’s got over 100 of them in his house. I don’t even know how he does it.      You know, I used to think it was just a hobby, but now I’m starting to wonder if it’s genetic. My mother was the same. She’d spend hours on a jigsaw and never once get frustrated.      Frustration? What are you talking about? I once had to give up on a jigsaw because I’d been staring at it for so long that I started seeing shapes where there weren’t any.      That’s probably the allergies. I had a really bad reaction to some kind of pollen last spring. I was trying to finish a jigsaw in the garden and suddenly I couldn’t breathe. My husband had to call an ambulance.      I can’t believe that. I mean, I’ve had a few allergies in my time, but nothing like that. Except maybe the time I tried to eat a new type of cheese and ended up in the ER.      I remember when I was a kid, my dad had a serious operation. It was a surgical operation, and I was so scared I couldn’t sleep for a week. Now I can’t even watch a documentary about it without getting anxious.      I had a friend who went through a similar thing. He had a surgical operation and the only thing he wanted to talk about for weeks was how his surgeon looked.

I can't believe we've got to this point with Moodle. I mean, it's been such a struggle trying to get the students to use it properly. It feels like we're fighting an uphill battle every time we introduce a new feature. I know what you mean. I've been trying to set up the new assignment module, and half the class didn't even know it existed. It’s like they’re still using the old system from last year. Exactly. And don’t get me started on the feedback section. It was supposed to streamline the process, but now I’m getting more emails from students asking for help with it than I do from actual questions about the material. It's like we’re teaching Moodle as much as we are the course content. I feel like I’m half a step behind every time I open the platform. Sometimes I wonder if we should just hand out PDFs and call it a day. I know, I’ve thought about that too. But then again, Moodle is supposed to make collaboration easier. I just wish the interface was less of a maze. I’ve had to spend more time figuring out how to navigate the system than actually preparing for lectures. I’ve been trying to set up some extra support sessions for the students. Maybe we can do a quick walkthrough on the basics, like how to submit assignments and check grades. That might help cut down on the confusion. That could work. I’ve been meaning to create a short video guide, but I keep putting it off. I’m worried it might come across as too basic or not helpful enough. Maybe it’s better to start small. We can do a 10-minute session where we walk through the key features. If the students see it in action, they might be more likely to use it. Yeah, that makes sense. I’ll draft a plan for the next week. I’ll also reach out to the IT department to see if they can provide any support or training materials. Perfect. And maybe we could stick together to present it. I know the students respond better when both of us are involved. That sounds like a solid plan. I’ll get started on the outline today. It’s just a shame we’re spending so much time on the tech side rather than the actual teaching.

So, I just got back from the airport, and I’m still feeling like I’ve been through a hurricane. Jetlag’s really kicking in. I’m so tired I could fall asleep standing up.      I can imagine. That flight from Barcelona must’ve been brutal. You’ve been away for a week now, right?      Yeah, just over a week. I was meant to be away for a research conference, but I got stuck in a last-minute meeting and ended up staying an extra day. It was ridiculous.      I’m sorry to hear that. You look like you’ve lost a few pounds. I mean, the jetlag and all that stress—must’ve taken a toll.      Oh, you don’t know the half of it. I feel like I’ve been running on empty for days. I’m just glad I’m home now. I’ve been trying to get back into my routine, but honestly, I’m still not fully there.      I get that. I’ve been trying to get back into my own routine after the baby came. It’s been a struggle, honestly. Between work and looking after the kid, I’m constantly on edge.      Oh, I can’t imagine how hard that must be. I’ve got a bit of a head start, but I’m still not quite used to the idea of having a baby around. It’s a bit surreal, isn’t it?      Definitely. I mean, it’s amazing, but it’s also exhausting. I had to cancel a few meetings last week because I just couldn’t keep up with the sleep schedule.      I hear you. I’m starting to think that maybe I should take a few weeks off work to adjust. I don’t want to burn out.      That’s a good idea. You’ve been working so hard lately, and I know how much you value your time. You deserve a break.      You’re right. I just need to figure out how to make it work. Speaking of which, we were supposed to go to that local dramatic performance next weekend, right?      Yeah, the one at the theatre downtown. I’ve been looking forward to it. I think it’s going to be a really good show.      I can’t wait. It’s been a while since we’ve had a proper night out. Maybe we can make it a little treat for ourselves?

So, I've been meaning to ask you, how do you manage to keep in touch with so many friends across the world? I mean, I’m more of a local kind of guy, even though I travel for work. It’s hard to keep up with what’s going on in all those different places.      Well, it helps that I’ve got this job where I translate and interpret. I’ve been working with people from all over—some from Iraq, some from the UK, some from Europe. It’s like I’m living in a small version of the world. Plus, I’ve got a lot of friends who are also in the translation business, so we keep in touch through LinkedIn and email. But honestly, it’s not just work. I’ve got a couple of friends in Libya, and I try to check in with them every few months. They’re all about the politics of oil down there. It’s a mess, but they’re still trying to make sense of it.      I can imagine. I’ve been reading a bit about the politics of oil—especially in places like Libya and Iraq. It’s always so complicated. You know, it’s like the same issues keep coming up, just in different forms. I wonder how it affects the young people there. You ever think about that?      Absolutely. It really does. The youth there are caught in this cycle of political instability and economic decline. I’ve spoken to a few young people who are trying to leave, but the visa process is so complicated. They need a lot of paperwork, and it’s not just about the law—it’s about the way the system is set up. I remember one colleague who tried to get a UK visa for his sister, but it took over a year. She finally got it, but only after they had to check her background with multiple agencies.      That’s terrible. I mean, I’ve got friends in the UK who have moved there and it was a lot of paperwork for them too, but it didn’t take as long. You must have some insight into how the visa system works. I’ve heard a lot about the 'Wahabi' issue—how it affects Muslim communities in the West. Do you think that’s a real problem or just something that's been exaggerated?

So, I just had to take a bite of that roast lamb, and it was...  exactly  what I expected. It was perfect. Not too dry, not too greasy. Just the right amount of herb and garlic underneath.      I'm glad to hear that. I thought it was good too, but I had to make sure it wasn't too overcooked. I mean, it's a roast lamb, not a steak. It needs time to rest.      Oh, I've made roast lamb many times, but it's always the same thing. You cook it to perfection, then you have to wait like an hour before you even dare to cut into it. I remember when I was a headmistress, I would have the whole staff in the dining room for dinner, and it was a ritual. The lamb was always the highlight.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? It’s not just about the food. It’s about the memory of the meal, the company, the atmosphere.      I agree. It’s funny how something so simple can bring people together. I remember when I was growing up in Edinburgh, my family always had a roast on Sundays, and it was just a tradition.      Yes, and I think that’s the beauty of it. It’s not just food. It’s about togetherness. You know, I’ve thought about doing a cruise with my friends, but I’m not sure. It’s expensive, and I don’t know if I’d like it.      I’m not sure about that either. I’ve always thought about it, but then I remember the TV in the dining room. I don’t think I’d be able to stand being on a boat for a week.      I think I’d go insane. I can’t stand being on a plane for more than five hours.      Well, I do have a Scottish tablet, though. It’s something I’ve had since I was a girl. I remember my mother used to use it to keep track of the weather and the tides. It’s a bit nostalgic, but I can’t part with it.      A Scottish tablet? That’s interesting. I’ve never heard of that before. Do you mean like a weather chart or something?      Yes, it's a kind of weather device. It's been in the family for generations. I think it's a bit of a relic, but it’s part of our history.

Alright, so I’ve been thinking—what’s up with us not having a proper fridge? I mean, we’ve got a freezer, but it’s not like we can just grab a sandwich in the middle of the night, is it?      Yeah, I know, it’s like we’re living in a hostel. I’ve had to go out and buy a loaf of bread just to have something to eat for lunch. And then what? We dump it in the freezer and forget about it. It’s ridiculous.      Honestly, I’m used to it. I grew up in Germany, and we never had a fridge at home. We just had a big old cupboard and a fridge that was, like, five years old. But I guess I’m used to living without one. It was weird at first, but now I just— shrugs —I’m alright.      You’re not from around here, are you? I mean, you’ve got that German accent, but you’re speaking English like you’ve been in the UK your whole life. Did you move here as a kid?      Yeah, I came over when I was eight. My parents got a job in Manchester, and they moved here. I’ve been here ever since. I never even thought about going back. I mean, I miss the food, but the people here? They’re just… different. I don’t know, it’s like they’re always shouting or something.      Yeah, but that’s Whitehaven. You know, it’s about an hour from Carlisle. I mean, it’s got its charms, but it’s definitely not the kind of place that puts you in a good mood. Especially not when you’re trying to get through uni and you’ve got no steady income.      I get where you’re coming from. I’m a TA, so I’ve got a bit more security, but I still have to worry about bills. I mean, I’ve got a flat with three of you, and it’s like trying to live with three different personalities.      Yeah, that’s us. Three people trying to live like we’ve got a budget. I mean, I’m unemployed, and I’m still trying to figure out what I’m going to do with my life. I’ve got a degree in history, but I don’t even know if I want to go into teaching or something else.

So, I’ve been thinking about what we’re going to do for Mum’s lesson... I was just at Morrisons and I saw a box of these really cute little chocolate cupcakes with a little bow on top. They look perfect for the half birthday celebration.      Oh, those look so nice! Are they the ones with the pink frosting? I saw them last week and thought they would be great for the class.      Yeah! And I was thinking, maybe we could also make some cookies? I saw a recipe for chocolate chip cookies in the magazine. They’re easy and the kids love them.      That sounds like a great idea. I can help with the baking, and I’ll bring some ingredients from home. Oh, and I found this really cool book about Tomodachi life while I was there. It’s about Japanese friendship and how people in Japan celebrate their relationships.      Tomodachi? That’s Japanese for "friend" or "friendship," isn’t it? I’ve heard of that term before. But how does it relate to Mum’s lesson?      Well, the lesson is about cultural diversity and friendships across the world. So I thought it would be a good idea to introduce the concept of Tomodachi and maybe have the kids create their own friendship bracelets or something. It’s a way to connect with people from different backgrounds.      That sounds fun! I’d love to make a friendship bracelet. I’ve seen some really cool ones online.      Oh, you can do that! We can have a little craft time after the lesson. And I was also thinking about the half birthday celebration. Maybe we can have a little party for the kids after the lesson.      That would be so much fun! I can help with the decorations. I have some balloons and streamers from last year.      I can bring the cake! I’ve got a chocolate cake in the fridge.      Perfect! I’ll bring the cupcakes and the cookies. And maybe we can even read the Tomodachi book together during the lesson. It’s a really nice way to connect with the kids.      I think that’ll make the lesson really special. I can’t wait to see how the kids react to the different ideas.      Wait, where’s the book? I thought it was in the car.      Oh, right! It’s still in the car. I’ll grab it on the way home.

So, what do you think about that new electric car my brother-in-law bought? I swear, it’s so quiet I almost thought he’d forgotten to turn it on.      Oh, I bet you were  so  excited when he finally got it. I mean, I’ve been telling him for years he should upgrade from that clunky old diesel. But I still can’t get over how fast it accelerates. It’s like he’s got a horse under the hood.      Yeah, I know what you mean. It’s like it’s  alive . But I’m still not convinced about the range. I mean, how do you know you’re not going to be left high and dry on the A1? I remember that time I had to charge in a remote village and had to wait for an hour for someone to come out.      That’s a story for another time. But honestly, I think the tech is getting better. My cousin just got one, and he’s been using it for months without a hitch. I mean, the only thing that’s still a bit of a mystery is how to fix it when it breaks. You can’t just pop the hood and fix it like a regular car.      I imagine that’s the downside of moving to the future. You know what I found funny, though? When I was trying to set up a Facebook group for the local car club, I noticed half the members were still on the old Facebook. It’s like they’re stuck in the past.      I know, right? I tried to explain to my uncle that you don’t have to be a teenager to use the new Facebook. But he just says, “It’s Facebook, not Instagram. My kids don’t even use it anymore.”      You know, I was thinking the other day about how the internet is changing everything. I mean, just last week, I got a message from a student who used to attend my lectures. She told me she’s now working in Norway, and she sends me articles from the Guardian via Facebook. It’s kind of crazy how much it’s changed our lives.      I know. I’ve been trying to get my dad to use Facebook more. He’s always been a bit skeptical. But I told him, “You don’t have to be on it all the time, just check in once in a while.”

So, I've been working my arse off all week. I had to do a load of stock shifts at the shop, and then there was this presentation for my course. I've been so tired, I've barely had time to eat properly.      Yup, I can’t even imagine. I’ve been stuck in lectures all week too. But at least I’ve got my own kitchen here. I’ve been cooking up a storm this week. Actually, I made this stew last night, it was pretty good.      You're a godsend. I haven’t had a proper meal in days. I just grab a sandwich and call it a day. I can't even remember the last time I had a decent roast dinner.      I know, I feel the same. But I thought I'd try to make something different today. I was watching  Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs  on the TV, which I know you don’t usually like, but I thought it might be a good way to relax. What do you think?      Hah, I’ve never really liked that film. It’s one of those things that seems wholesome, but I can’t get past the plot. I mean, it feels like it’s trying too hard to be cute. But I guess it’s good for kids.      It’s not that bad. I think it’s got some hidden meanings. Like, the whole town being in a bubble and everything. It’s sort of a metaphor for how we live our lives, or something. Maybe about the environment? I don’t know. But it’s got a good message.      Well, I’m not sure about the hidden meanings, but I’ll give it a try. I’ve been wanting to watch it again. I think I’ve missed something. Maybe I’ll have to explain it to you properly later.      Yeah, I’d love to hear your take on it. Do you think there’s anything about it that’s actually relevant today? Like, how people are connected to the things they consume?      I guess so. It’s about how everything is linked, in a way. Like, if the food is coming from the sky, then it’s like our food systems are just as fake as the clouds in the film. It’s a bit of an odd analogy, but it makes you think.

You know, I’ve been here a few times for meetings, but it’s still weird to be in Finland. I mean, I’ve spent most of my life in the UK and Germany. Liverpool to Salzkotten, it’s a long way from here.      Yeah, I can imagine. I’ve driven through here a few times too. Got stuck in a snowstorm last winter, had to wait for hours. But it’s a beautiful place, even if it’s a bit quiet.      That’s the thing about Finland. It’s peaceful, but sometimes you miss the energy of a city. Speaking of which, what’s the vibe like in Liverpool these days? I’ve been back a couple of times, and things seem to be changing.      Oh, you’re not wrong. Liverpool’s gone through a lot. When I was growing up, it was different. The 80s and 90s—there was a lot of struggle, but then came the football—Eurgh, I still get nostalgic for that era.      I remember that. I was in my late teens when the Reds were at their peak. It was a national thing. But then came New Labour, Tony Blair, and all that political change. You know, the shift from the old Labour to the new. It was a big deal at the time.      Yeah, I remember that. I was a young cabbie then, so I didn’t really get all the political jargon, but I could feel the shift. People were talking about it in the taxi ranks. It was like the whole country was trying to move forward, but some people didn’t like it.      Exactly. I think the key was the change in rhetoric—New Labour, ‘Third Way’ policies, less socialist, more market-friendly. It was a big move from the traditional Labour party. Do you think it worked?      I don’t know. I think it kept the country stable, but it also lost some of its identity. You know, Labour used to stand for something more. But maybe that’s just me. I’ve always been more of a socialist at heart, even if I didn’t always vote for the right people.      That’s a fair point. I think politics is complicated. It’s not just about policies; it’s about how people see themselves and their place in the world. But I’ll admit, the ‘Third Way’ did help the economy a bit.

So, I was just going through some old BNC recordings the other day, and I found this one from the 80s. It’s so fascinating how people spoke back then! You know, they used to say “innit” and “chuffed” all the time. It’s like a whole different dialect.      Yeah, I remember that. I’ve been studying a bit of Welsh in my spare time, so I can tell you there are a lot of similarities and differences. You know, like how “chuffed” is pretty much the Welsh equivalent of “proud” or “happy.”      That’s true. And I think you still hear some of that in parts of London, especially in the East End. I mean, Aylesbury and London are quite different, but sometimes you can catch a few old habits.      Definitely. I grew up in Abergavenny, so I’ve always heard the Welsh influence. Sometimes I feel like I’m caught between two worlds—English and Welsh. It’s funny, isn’t it? You can’t really say you’re from one place without acknowledging the other.      I can see that. You ever think about moving back to Wales? I mean, I know it’s not London, but the lifestyle is different. I’ve been meaning to visit for a while. Last year, I even applied for a short-term visa just to see what it’s like.      Oh, really? I’d love to hear about your experience. I’ve been thinking about going to Spain for a while now. I have this dream of living in a small town near the coast, maybe something like San Sebastian. I’ve never been, but I’ve read so much about it.      Spain sounds amazing. I’ve always wanted to go to the Maldives. I remember reading about it in a LinkedIn article once—like, it’s this perfect place to relax. But I’m scared of flying. I know it’s a cliché, but I just can’t get over the fear of being in the air.      That’s so relatable. I remember my first flight was a nightmare. I was so nervous I started crying. But once I got on the plane, it was fine. Maybe it’s just the way we’re wired to be scared of falling?      True. I’ve been thinking about getting over it, but honestly, I’m still not sure. I’ve been trying to watch some travel vloggers on YouTube to get inspired, but it’s not helping much.

So, I’ve been thinking about what to cook for Christmas. I wanted to do something a bit different from the usual roast dinner. Maybe try a few festive dishes from different countries? I mean, it’s Christmas, right? Why not mix it up a bit?      That sounds like a great idea. I love that kind of thing. Though I’ve been meaning to ask — have you got any tattoos? I remember you said you were going to get one last year. Did you end up doing it?      Yeah, I did. It’s a small one on my wrist — a simple Celtic knot. I’ve been meaning to show it off more. I guess I just didn’t feel like it was the right time. But now, with the holidays coming up, I think I’m ready to embrace it more.      That’s a cool design. I’ve always thought tattoos are a great way to express yourself, even if they’re small. I’ve got one on my forearm — a little fern, actually. It’s a reminder of my hometown in the countryside.      A fern? That’s kind of peaceful. I can’t imagine having one like that. My roommate’s got a huge one, like, a dragon or something. It’s like he’s trying to be a pirate or something.      He’s got a sense of humor. But seriously, I think it’s a good way to have something that stays with you forever. Speaking of which, I heard you’ve been working with some interns recently. How are they doing?      Yeah, it’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. Some are great, others are… well, not so much. But it’s part of the job. I’ve been trying to get them up to speed, and I think they’re starting to get the hang of things. Although, I still need to remind them to wash their hands after using the bathroom.
