Oh, that’s the one! He was so upset. I mean, 15 over? That’s not even that bad.      He was so embarrassed. He kept saying it wasn’t his fault; he just got distracted by the radio.      I think we’re all just bad drivers, no matter how much we try to be responsible.

Hey, thanks for coming over! I’ve been dying to catch up since you went on holiday. How was it?      Oh, it was great! I spent a few days in Cornwall with my mum. The weather was absolutely perfect, and we had such a nice chat. It was nice to get away and just relax, you know?      That sounds wonderful. I’ve been a bit stuck in the house lately, trying to get things sorted here. Oh, and I was just wondering—do you think we should start redecorating the living room? It’s been a while since we’ve touched it up.      Honestly, I think it’s about time. You know how much I love a fresh coat of paint. But I’d need a bit of help, to be honest. I’m not the most talented in the world with a brush.      No worries, I can handle that. I’ve been thinking about doing some work on the kitchen too. The tiles are starting to look a bit worn. Should we tackle both at the same time or take it one at a time?      I think one at a time would be better. I don’t want us to get overwhelmed. Maybe we can start with the kitchen this weekend. I’ve got some ideas for new cabinet hardware, and I think it would really brighten things up.      That sounds good. I’ll check the supplies store this week and see what we can get. Oh, by the way, how’s work been for you? I know you’ve been busy with the new mental health ward at the hospital.      It’s been a bit intense, honestly. We’ve had a few new patients come in, and it’s been really challenging, but rewarding. I met this one guy the other day who was really open about his struggles. It was incredible to see how much he’s come on since starting treatment.      That’s amazing. I can’t imagine how tough it must be, but I admire the way you handle it. I hope you’re taking some time for yourself too. You deserve it.      I try, but between work and the house, it’s hard to find balance. I was thinking about going to that yoga class I mentioned last week. Would you like to come with me? It might help me relax a bit.      That sounds like a great idea.

So, I just heard from Helen yesterday. She’s really struggling. The cancer has spread again, and they’re talking about more aggressive treatment. It’s so hard to watch, you know?      I know, it’s heartbreaking. I saw her at the café last week, and she looked so tired. She tried to make small talk, but it was obvious she wasn’t feeling well.      Yeah, and she’s been so withdrawn lately. I mean, she used to be the one who always had something to say. Now she just sits in silence most of the time. It’s like part of her is gone.      It’s awful. I’ve been trying to reach out, but she’s not really responding. I feel like I should do more, but I don’t know what to say.      It’s not about what you say, it’s about being there. I think she’s just scared. The doctors keep giving her different options, and she’s not sure which one is the right one.      I know. I remember reading somewhere that people with terminal illnesses often feel like they’re burdening others. She might be thinking that way too.      Exactly. And then there’s her kids. They’re both away at university, and she’s worried about them. She doesn’t want to be a burden.      I wish there was something we could do. Maybe just keep her company, make her feel like she’s not alone.      I think that’s all we can do. It’s not about fixing it, it’s about supporting her. I’ve been thinking about getting her some nice books or something. You know, things that make her feel comfortable.      That sounds good. I could help with that. I mean, we’re both lecturers, so we know how to pick out something meaningful.      Yeah, and maybe we can take her out for a walk in the village. The weather’s been so nice lately. It might help her feel a bit better.      I’d like that. I’ve also been thinking about the houses for sale in the village. The planning application is goin’ through, and if it gets approved, there might be some new developments.      Yeah, I heard about that. Some people are excited about it, others are worried about the impact on the community.      I think it’s a bit of both. It could bring in more people, more businesses, but maybe also more traffic and noise.

So, I've been thinking, do you ever just get fed up with the same old stuff? Like, I don’t know, the way the maintenance here is always breaking down, or the fact that the student flat we’re supposed to be guarding is like a warzone half the time.      Oh, I’ve been there, mate. I swear, it’s not just the flats — it’s everything. I mean, I love my job, but sometimes I just can’t shake this feeling that we’re wasting our time. Like, the way the system is set up, we’re just stuck doing the same thing every day. I mean, I don’t even mind the security part, but the way we’re treated? It’s like we’re just cogs in a machine.      Yeah, I feel that. I mean, the pay’s not bad, but the hours? They’re relentless. I’ve been working late shifts for weeks now, and I’m just not getting enough sleep. I keep telling myself it’s for the job, but honestly, I’m starting to think I’d rather be doing something else. Like, maybe I’d be better off working in a shop or something. At least then I’d get some real break time.      I get that. I’ve actually been thinking about taking a gap year, you know? Just to see the world, or maybe even go back to studying. I was meant to finish my degree last year, but then the pandemic hit, and everything just… fell apart. I didn’t want to go back to university, but now I’m wondering if I should. I mean, it’s not like I’ve got much else to lose, right?      Honestly, I can see the appeal. I mean, I’ve always wanted to travel, but I’m too scared to take the leap. I mean, I have this job, and I’ve got a mortgage. I can’t just cut my losses and run off to some faraway land. Not without a plan, anyway.      I know, it’s not easy. But you know what? Sometimes the only way to find out what you really want is to just try. I’m not saying I’m going to quit the job tomorrow, but I’m starting to see that maybe I’m not as stuck as I thought. I just need to figure out what I want next.

You know, I was in Antwerp last week, and I bumped into this guy I went to uni with. It was wild—like, I hadn’t seen him since we graduated, and now we were both in the same city, just hanging out at a Christmas market. I mean, it’s not like we were on the same course or anything, but it was still a weird coincidence.      Oh, I’ve had some interesting run-ins with people from back home. I was at a package tour in Barcelona, and I met this old guy who turned out to be my cousin’s ex. We had the most awkward conversation about how he’d moved to Spain and hadn’t kept in touch. I left the table immediately.      I think I’ve had the opposite. I was at a Christmas market in Herne Bay—wait, no, that’s not a market. I was at the seaside, and I met this guy who said he was from Dorset. I immediately thought, "Oh no, here we go," but he ended up being one of my old uni mates. We ended up staying in touch, even though we’ve never met in person before.      That’s so cool. I feel like meeting people from your past is one of the best things about traveling. But seriously, I did have this moment at a Christmas market in Brighton—wait, that’s where we are now. I was there last year, and I saw my friend from uni, and we had a proper catch-up. It was like a scene from a movie.      Sounds like you’re getting all the luck. I’m the one who’s still waiting for my first "coincidental" reunion. I was in London the other day, and I went to that new café on the seafront. I ended up sitting next to a guy who was just telling me about the traffic in Brighton. I asked him how he knew so much about it, and he said he used to work as a delivery driver.      That’s the thing with Brighton. You can’t really get lost, but you can definitely get stuck in traffic. I used to work in Harlow, and I’d drive down here every weekend. It’s like the M23 just decides it wants to be your enemy.      I’ve been to the countryside in Dorset a few times—my friends and I rented a caravan.

Hey, I just saw the news about the equality vote in Ireland. I was watching it on the telly when I was supposed to be doing homework, but it was so interesting. I didn’t even realize it was happening until my mom started explaining it to me.      Oh, really? I saw that too, but I didn’t really get it. What’s the vote about exactly?      It’s about marriage equality, isn’t it? Like, allowing same-sex couples to get married. I think it was a referendum, right?      Oh right, I remember something about that. I mean, I don’t really know much about politics, but I know that Ireland is pretty traditional when it comes to stuff like that. I guess this was a big shift.      Yeah, totally. My teacher said it was a huge deal. Like, it’s not just about marriage, it’s about equality for everyone. I think it was the first time Ireland had a vote on something like this.      That’s crazy. I mean, I get it, but I never really thought about it that much. I’ve got a toddler, so I’m more focused on things like changing nappies and trying not to fall asleep while she’s crying.      I can’t imagine that. I mean, I’m still in school, so I’m not dealing with all that. But I guess every parent has their own kind of stress.      Yeah, it’s a different kind of stress. I mean, I had my own wedding, and I remember my mom being so embarrassed about it. She kept saying how it was “not how it’s supposed to be.” I mean, come on, it was just a party.      Oh no! I can imagine that. My mom’s always joking about how she tried to plan the perfect party for my birthday, but it ended up being a complete disaster. She told me I was the only one who liked it.      Ha! I know what you mean. My mom’s always trying to be the best at everything, but she’s also the most embarrassing person you could ever meet. She once tried to make a cake for my toddler’s first birthday and ended up burning it.      That’s not even funny. I mean, I can see it now. A charred cake with melted icing.      Exactly! And she kept saying it was “a masterpiece.”

Well, I suppose I should’ve learned more about lathe tools when I was younger. I remember when I used to make things with my dad’s old lathe. He was a real craftsman, always explaining how the different tools worked. But I never really got into it. I mean, I liked the idea of making things, but I reckon I just wasn’t cut out for the precision. A lathe requires a lot of patience, don’t you think?      I remember something like that from when I was a kid too. My dad used to do some woodwork, even built a shelf for our living room. But I never really got the hang of it. My hands are too clumsy, I guess. Though I do like the idea of making things with my own hands, even if I’m not the best at it. It gives you a sense of accomplishment, doesn’t it?      Oh, I’d say it’s more than just accomplishment—it’s about the process. I once had to do a project for my job, and I had to design a model using various tools, including a lathe. It was a bit of a challenge, but it was good to get back into the rhythm of it all. You really have to be methodical with a lathe, and that kind of structure helps you focus. Though I’m not sure if I’d ever want to work with one again—too much precision for my taste.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? I think I’d rather be out in the garden with my hands in the soil than trying to make a perfect piece of wood. Though I did try to grow a few vegetables last year. Not sure if I was any good at that either. My tomato plants were all scorched, and the potatoes didn’t even sprout. My wife said I must’ve been concentrating too hard on the weather.      You mentioned tomatoes before, didn’t you? I remember you trying to grow your own. You even tried to use a microwave to keep them warm. I didn’t think that was a good idea, but I suppose it’s better than nothing.      Oh, I know, I know. I thought it might help them grow faster. I’m not entirely sure how that worked, but I’ll be the first to admit I was just trying to be clever.

So, I was just thinking about that mirror-writing thing in the paper the other day. You know, like when people write backwards so they can read it in a mirror? It’s funny how some people still do it, even with all the technology we have now.      Yeah, I remember when I was a kid, my granddad used to write letters that way. He said it helped him focus. I’ve never been able to do it, though. I guess I’m just too lazy to bother.      Oh, I used to do it all the time when I was a teacher. It was part of my handwriting practice. I found it helped with motor skills, especially when teaching children to write. But honestly, I’ve never liked the way it looks. It’s just… too messy.      I used to think it was cool. Like, if you could write backwards, then maybe you could write in code? Although I guess that’s more of a criminal thing, isn’t it?      Definitely. I mean, I’ve heard stories about people using mirror-writing to communicate secretly. But I think it’s more of a novelty now. Still, I can’t help but think about the banks and how they’re always talking about debt. Do you think we’re ever going to get out of this financial mess?      Honestly, I’ve seen enough of the world to know that people will always find a way to get back on their feet. It’s just a matter of time. But I also think the housing market is a big part of it. I remember when house prices were at their peak, and now they’ve dropped so much. It’s like people are still trying to catch up.      I can’t even imagine what it’s like to be a first-time buyer now. My parents bought their house in the early 2000s, and even then, it was a struggle. I can’t help but feel that the government should be doing more to help people out, especially with all the charges for plastic bags.      I agree. It’s just another way for the government to make money, right? They charge for plastic bags, but then they also increase taxes on everything else. It’s a bit of a cycle. Though I have to say, I think the cat story in the news is more interesting.

Oh, I can't believe how long they've been playing with those Lego Ninjago sets. I thought they'd be done by now, but they're still building that giant dragon! It's like they've got some kind of obsession.      Yeah, I don’t know what’s gotten into them. I mean, it's not like they’ve been reading any books or anything. They just sit there for hours building and then they go into Minecraft and create entire worlds. It's like they're living in a different universe.      I know, right? I tried to get them to read a story last night, and they just stared at me like I was from another planet. It was ridiculous. I think they’d rather be building castles and fighting dragons than read about anything real.      I can only imagine what they’re creating in Minecraft. I’ve heard they built a whole city with shops, roads, and even a castle. They must have spent hours planning it out.      Yeah, I think they even named it "Ninjago City." They said it’s the best city in the world. I don’t know how they come up with all that stuff. It’s like they have a whole imagination going on.      I think they just enjoy the freedom of creating their own world. There’s no rules, no limits. They can be a king, a warrior, a builder, whatever they want. It’s kind of cool, in a way.      I guess it’s about giving them space to explore their interests. But I still worry that they’re not spending enough time on things like reading or learning new skills. I mean, it’s fun, but there has to be a balance.      I agree. I think they’re getting a lot out of those games and toys, but I do miss the days when they used to read books and tell me stories. It was so much fun.      I miss that too. I remember when I used to read to them before bed. It was like a little ritual. Now it's all about Legos and Minecraft. I wonder if they even remember what it’s like to read a real story.      Maybe we can start a reading time again. Maybe something simple, like a bedtime story every night. I think they might enjoy it again, especially if we read something fun and engaging.

Well, I've been meaning to talk to you both about how much I missed you all on our recent holiday. It was such a beautiful time, wasn't it?      Oh, I know, it was amazing. We got to visit that little seaside town you'd been wanting to go to for years. I still can't get over how clean the beach was.      And how the fish was, honestly. I’ve never had such fresh seafood. You remember that place where they grilled the fish on the beach?      Oh, I remember. You were so excited about it. I think you even tried to catch a fish with the net, didn't you?      Oh, don’t remind me. I was about to catch one when it slipped through my fingers and swam away. I was so close!      You were a bit too eager. I think you were more determined than skilled.      Well, it’s not like you weren’t trying. Honestly, I’ve never seen anyone so excited about a fish.      Yeah, I know. I guess I was just really eager to try something new.      Speaking of new things, have you two thought about what you’re going to do this weekend? I know you mentioned something about a picnic.      Yes, we were thinking of going to the countryside. The weather’s been so nice, and I think we could all use a bit of fresh air.      That sounds perfect. I’ve been meaning to take a walk in the woods near here. It’s so peaceful.      I’d love to come. I’ve been needing to get out of the house for a bit. My studies are keeping me busy, but I miss being out and about.      Well, let’s make it a family picnic then. We can bring the food, set up a blanket, and just enjoy each other’s company.      That sounds like a plan. I’ll bring the sandwiches.      And I’ll bring the music. I’ve got this old radio I found in my grandmother’s attic that plays some really good tunes.      Perfect. I love that idea. It'll be like old times, just like when we were kids.      Yeah, it really will. I think we've all needed a little bit of that lately.      Definitely. It's great to be together like this.      And I’m so glad we can still do things like this.

So, I just got this sandwich from the café, and it’s the best thing since sliced bread. I mean, it’s got this giant burger, a side of fries, and a drink. It’s like a meal in itself.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I tried the chicken wrap, but honestly, it felt like I ate a whole chicken. I’ve never been a big fan of wraps, but I guess I’ll give them a second chance.      Honestly, you two are making me hungry. I just had a salad, but it was so bland. I wish we had more options here. I mean, I love food, but sometimes the stuff in supermarkets just doesn’t cut it.      Yeah, I feel you. I remember when I was in school, we used to make our own sandwiches at lunch. It was always a mess, but it was fun. Remember when we had that lunchtime game where we had to guess what each other’s sandwich was?      Oh, totally! I still remember that time when I thought you had a mushroom sandwich, and it turned out to be a chicken one. You were like, “No way, that’s not even close!”      That was so funny. I remember trying to figure out what yours was and thinking it was something totally different. I’m glad we don’t have to do that now.      Speaking of school, have you guys heard about the new prefects? I heard they’re all a bit strict. I mean, not too bad, but some of them are like,  “If you don’t finish your homework, you’re in trouble” —even if you’re not doing it because your dog ate it.      Oh, I know that one. My brother’s a prefect, and he’s always threatening to give out detentions for things that are  not  even punishable. Like, once he gave a detention to someone for being late  three  times in a row.      That sounds harsh. I mean, I get that they have to be strict, but it’s not like we’re soldiers. I think it’s a bit unfair. Plus, I heard some of the teachers are really on the fence about the new rules.      I don’t know. I mean, maybe they’re trying to change things for the better. I just hope they don’t go too far.      Yeah, I agree. But I also think some of the stuff they’re doing is kind of overkill.

Hey, have you seen the new physics teacher? I swear, she’s like a superhero with a lab coat.      Oh, I saw her too! She’s so intense, but in a cool way. I mean, she actually  gets  us. I think she’s trying to make physics less scary.      Yeah, I totally agree. I used to think physics was just about equations and stuff, but she makes it all make sense. Like, she even explained why the moon pulls the tides in a way that makes sense.      That’s what I like about her. She also makes us laugh. I caught her once trying to explain Newton’s laws and she said, “If you drop a melon and a pea from the same height, they’ll hit the ground at the same time—unless the melon is a  muppet .” And we all cracked up.      Oh my god, that’s brilliant! I wish our form tutor was like that. She’s so boring. I mean, she just stands there and reads the same notes every day. I think she’s half asleep most of the time.      Yeah, I know. I mean, we’ve all got to be in her class, but it’s just so… predictable. I feel like I could take notes for her.      Haha, you should! You know what I found funny though? She made us watch the film  17 Again  for English. I thought it was a romantic comedy, but it turned out to be about a kid who gets sent back to high school.      Oh, I watched it too! It was kinda okay, but I couldn’t stop thinking about how much I miss being 17. Like, I remember that time when I accidentally spilled my lunch on my history essay. My teacher got so mad, she made me sit in the corner for the rest of the class.      Wait, did you? That’s hilarious! I once got sent to the corner for writing  Harry Potter  in my English assignment. I didn’t even finish the story!      Oh no, that’s so you. But I think the teacher got it in the end. She said something like, “You have a creative mind, but you need to focus on the task at hand.”      Yeah, I guess that’s what they all say. But we’re still kids, right? I mean, we’ve got a long way to go before we’re actually adults.

So, what’s the word on the street? You lot haven’t been seen around for ages. I thought you were all off to Transylvania last month.      We were, but I got stuck in a motorway jam for three hours. I think the van was pretending to be a duck.      You should’ve taken the train, like the rest of us. I got there in two and a half hours. And the countryside was  perfect .      You’re a café owner, of course you’d have a train pass. What about you, Ross? You’re still in London?      Yeah, still working at the café. You know, the one with the weird lights and the guy who thinks he’s a DJ.      He still thinks he’s a DJ. I tried to explain to him that you can’t play music in a café without a permit, but he just waved a pen in the air like it was a microphone.      It’s not that bad. He’s got a good eye for coffee. And the clientele are mostly students. They just want something to sip on while they study.      It’s not like you’re not used to that. You’re a baker, for heaven’s sake. You must have people knocking on your door every morning.      Yeah, but I’ve got a bit of a reputation. If you come in looking like you’ve been crying, I’ll make you a cup of tea and a scone.      You’re not the only one with a reputation. I run a café, and I’ve got customers who’ve been coming in for years. Some even bring their kids.      Speaking of families, when are you going to crack on with your plans to move to Australia?      Any day now. I’ve got a job lined up in Brisbane. Plus, I’ve been learning some Aussie expressions. You know, like  arvo  and  barbie .      Are you sure you can say  barbie  without sounding like a tourist?      It’s not like you can say  chips  without sounding like a posh Londoner. You’re the one who said  crisps  in the café.      Oh, come on, I used to say  chips  as a kid. It was just easier to say them as  crisps  when I got to university.      I think you’re all missing out. I’ve got a plan to go to the Lake District this summer.

Okay, I think I’ve got everything sorted for the party tomorrow. The decorations are all up, the food is ready, and the music playlist is set. I think we’ll be fine.      But Mommy, can we have cake? I want to eat cake at the party.      Yeah, I want cake too. I think I saw some cookies in the fridge. Can we have those?      Of course you can, but the cake is for the party. Let’s save it for when we actually have guests. Now, about the music—do you remember the song we were talking about earlier?      Oh, the one with the rainbow? You said it reminded you of Alice in Wonderland.      Yes! That’s the one. I think it’s called "Rainbow Connection," and it’s from the movie  The Little Prince . It’s a bit cheesy, but I think it’ll go well with the theme of the party. I’ve got the playlist ready on my phone.      Can we play the aerial hoop too? I saw it in the living room. It looks fun.      Oh, you mean the one with the big circle? That’s the one I got for the photoshoot! I thought we could use it for some fun family photos. But maybe not at the party. It might be too messy.      Can we still do it? I want to be in the photo with the hoop!      Maybe after the party. There’s a muddy obstacle course set up in the garden too. I thought it would be a good way to keep everyone active. But if you’re too tired, we can skip it.      I’m not tired. I can do the obstacle course. I can jump over the log and run through the mud!      I can do that too! I’ll run like a cheetah!      That’s the spirit. I think we’ll have a great time. Just remember, if you see anyone swearing at the party, you tell me right away. It’s not nice.      But I don’t know what swearing is. Is it like when you say "muddy" or "obstacle"?      No, it’s when people say bad words. Like, "damn" or "crap." Just make sure to keep it clean, okay?      I know. I don’t like bad words. They make me sad.      That’s great. I’m so glad you’re both excited for the party. It’ll be fun, and we can take some family photos too.

So, I was just telling the lads about the time I tried to park my car in the village and ended up in the field. Blimey, I thought I’d found a shortcut, but it turned out to be a cow path!      That sounds like something you’d do, Bob. I remember when I was your age, I once tried to ride my bike to the shops and ended up in a hedge. My mum was beside herself!      Those days are a distant memory. I was too busy teaching to get into such scrapes. Though I do recall one time when I accidentally locked myself out of the school and had to wait for the janitor to let me in.      Yeah, and I think I remember that. Mr. Johnson was always the one to help out. He was a real gentle giant.      Wait, were you the teacher who used to bring in those weird cookies?      Oh, you mean the ones I made for the staff meetings? I’ve still got the recipe in my old notebook. It was a disaster, though. Half of them ended up in the bin.      I’ve seen worse. My wife once tried to make apple pie and ended up with something that looked more like a rock than a pie. She’s still not talking about it.      That’s nothing. I tried to bake a cake once and it turned into a volcano. I had to call the fire brigade.      No way! That’s insane!      I would have been so scared. I’d be running out of the house with a towel!      Well, I reckon we’re all guilty of a few disasters in our time. I tried to make a pizza once, and it ended up being more like a cardboard box.      You had the wrong ingredients, Bob. You used sugar instead of flour.      I remember that. You were so proud of it, and then you ate it and nearly had a heart attack.      That was the best pizza I ever had. It had a crunch to it.      So, what’s the food you’re making now?      Chocolate roulade and pizza. It’s a feast! I think we’ll all be full to the brim.      I love chocolate roulade! I’ve never had it before.      That’s a shame. It’s a classic. I used to make it for the kids when I was teaching.

So, Dad, I was thinking about those old recordings we used to make in the garden when I was a kid. You remember? We used to record the sounds of the birds, the squirrels, even the wind. I still have that old cassette player in the attic. Maybe we could do something like that again?      That sounds brilliant, really. I’ve been meaning to get back into that kind of stuff. I’ve got this new app that turns your voice into a kind of ambient sound track. We could even add some of the garden berries we picked last week. You know how they sound when you drop them?      Actually, I found a few of those berries in the shed the other day. I thought they were left over from last summer. I didn’t know they were still good. Maybe I should try making some jam with them?      Oh, you should! I’ve been wanting to try some berry jam for ages. And the weather’s been so nice lately, it’s the perfect time. I was thinking of taking some over to Mrs. Jenkins’ place this weekend—she always says she puts a few in her tea.      I was just watching a documentary about the rhythm of the seasons. It made me think about how much of our lives are influenced by the weather. You know, like the way we set our routines around it. I couldn’t help but think of Winston Churchill at times—how he used to talk about the weather in his speeches.      Yeah, I remember him talking about the weather at some of his speeches. It’s strange how something so simple can be such a big part of people’s lives. I think I’ve started using the weather more as a way to plan my day. Like, if it’s going to be cold, I’ll make a bigger breakfast.      That’s a good point. I’ve been trying to get into the habit of making a proper breakfast instead of just toast and coffee. I even found a few old cookbooks in the attic—there were some recipes from the 70s that I’ve been trying out. They’re not bad, actually.      That’s the spirit! I go to a few lectures on English literature and linguistics at the local college, and I’ve been really into how language evolves with time.

So, I heard you've been teaching English abroad again? How’s the gig going?      It's been good, honestly. I’m teaching at a language school in Kraków, which is actually pretty nice. The students are mostly from the local area, and some are even from nearby towns. I’ve got a few repeat students, which is always reassuring. Plus, the pay isn't bad for a part-time job.      That’s great to hear. I used to teach in Cambridge, but those days are long behind me. I’m just trying to get through the week now. I’ve been thinking about getting back into teaching, but I’m not sure if I have the energy. Between the unemployment and the pension situation, I’m just not sure what’s going to happen next.      I can imagine. I think the system is just so broken in the UK, especially for people like you, who never worked full-time. I mean, I’m lucky to be in a lower managerial role, but even then, I have to deal with student loans, and I don’t even know if I’ll get them repaid. It’s so frustrating.      It is. I’ve been thinking about pensions, too. I never worked enough to qualify for a proper one. I remember my parents had a decent pension, but I think it was because they were in the public sector. It’s so unfair. I don’t even know what I’m going to do if I don’t get a proper state pension. Maybe I’ll just have to live off savings, which I don’t really have.      I know exactly how you feel. I’ve been trying to get a better job for a while now, but every time I apply, the requirements are too high. It’s like they only want people with experience, but how can you get experience if you can’t get a job? I think I’m going to try and get a teaching certificate in Poland. The system seems more flexible there. Maybe I can work here for a bit.      That’s a good idea. I’ve been thinking about working abroad too. Maybe in the EU, or somewhere in Eastern Europe. I’ve heard about the MOT process here, and it’s not like the UK. I can go through it on my own if I need to.

So, I heard you've been thinking about university courses again. Are you still leaning towards Human Sciences or maybe something else?      Yeah, honestly, I’m still torn between Human Sciences and Maths. I like the idea of studying human behavior and psychology, but I’m also really good at Maths and I’m thinking about doing something more technical. What about you? Still on track for Human Sciences?      Yeah, I think I’m pretty much set on that. I’ve been reading some stuff about it, and it seems like it could be a good fit for me. But I’m not sure yet if I want to go into research or maybe something more applied. What’s your plan for next year?      I’m going to apply to both. It’s a bit of a gamble, but I figure if I get into one, I can always take a year out or do something else if it doesn’t work out. I’ve been thinking about doing some work experience in the social sector too, maybe in a charity or something like that.      That sounds like a solid plan. I’ve been thinking about doing some cooking classes in my free time. I’ve always loved cooking, and maybe it could be a way to combine it with my studies. Do you cook?      Mate, I can barely boil an egg without burning it. But I’ve been trying to get better. I’ve been watching some YouTube tutorials and actually, I’ve managed to make a decent risotto this week. Not perfect, but it’s a start.      That’s impressive! I’ve been thinking about doing a course in culinary arts, but I’m not sure if it’s worth it. I mean, I’m not sure if I want to go into professional cooking. It’s just a hobby for now.      I get that. But if you ever want to do something like that, I’d be up for cooking together. I think it’s a great way to relax. Speaking of which, have you been drinking much lately?      Honestly, not really. I’ve been trying to cut back. It’s not that I don’t like it—my rugby team does a few drinks after matches, but I’ve been feeling a bit guilty about it. I think I’ll stick to one or two drinks at most.

Well, I've been reading this article about the new tax changes they’re planning to introduce next year. I think it’s going to have a big impact on people like us, especially with the rising cost of living.      Really? I didn’t know there were any changes coming up. I thought the government was just delaying things for a bit. What’s the big news?      They’re talking about increasing the income tax threshold. It’s supposed to take some of the pressure off middle-income earners, but I don’t think it’s enough. The inflation rate is still high, and the real value of money is going down.      I can see that. I’ve been teaching English for a while now, and I’ve noticed more people are worried about their finances, especially the younger generation. They’re starting off with more debt than ever before.      Yeah, I remember when I first started working. The tax system was simpler, and people had more control over their money. These days, I feel like the government is regulating more and more, and it’s hard to know what’s fair or not.      I agree. I think there’s a real disconnect between the policies they’re pushing and what the people actually need. I’ve talked to a few students about this, and they’re confused about how the tax system works. It’s not just about numbers—it's about how people live their lives.      That’s a good point. I used to explain things to my kids when they were younger, and I found that making it relatable helped. Instead of just quoting figures, I’d talk about what the changes meant for their future.      Maybe I should do that. I’ve been trying to simplify my lessons, but I think it’s important to make sure the students understand the bigger picture. If they don’t understand how money works, they won’t be able to make informed decisions later on.      That’s exactly the mindset I had. I always believed that if you understand the system, you can navigate it better. It’s not just about saving money—it’s about knowing your rights and responsibilities as a citizen.      I’ve been thinking about writing an article or maybe even a blog about this. People need to know how to protect themselves in this new economic climate.

I just had the most frustrating meeting today. You know how it is—when you think you’ve got everything sorted, and then someone throws a curveball. It was about the new project we’re launching, and there was this confusion about the timeline. I spent half the meeting explaining the same thing again and again. Oh, I know exactly how you feel. I had something similar at work last week. I was presenting a report to the head of the department, and halfway through, someone asked a question that completely redirected the conversation. I had to backtrack, and it was so stressful. I just wanted to get through it without any hiccups. Yeah, it’s like you’re always trying to keep everyone on the same page, but sometimes you just can’t. It’s exhausting. I’m starting to think I should maybe take a step back and map out the project more clearly for next time. Maybe even get some feedback from the team beforehand. That sounds like a good idea. I always tell my team, "If you have a question, ask it early, not during the presentation." But, of course, they listen to me more when I don’t have a timetable to meet. It’s funny how priorities shift depending on the situation. Oh, I know. I’m always the one trying to keep the ball moving. I guess that’s part of being a project co-ordinator. You have to be proactive, even when it’s not the most enjoyable part of the job. But honestly, I love my job. I just wish sometimes the stress didn’t come with it. I can see how you’d feel that way. I used to get so stressed when there were unexpected changes, but over time, I learned to be more flexible. It’s not always easy, but you adjust. Speaking of which, how’s your family? I haven’t heard from you in a while. Oh, they’re all well. My sister came to visit last week. We had a great time, though it was a bit chaotic. She brought her kids, and we ended up cooking like five meals in one day. It was a proper family reunion. That sounds lovely. I miss having family visits. I’ve been so busy with work that I haven’t really had time to catch up. I think I need to make more space for that.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that time we tried to cook that lasagna and ended up with a fire? It was chaos, I tell you.      Oh, don’t even start! I remember you tried to make the sauce and burned the whole thing. I had to rush in with a fire extinguisher.      Yeah, that was a classic. I swear, if you had a fire extinguisher in every kitchen, you’d be set for life. But, hey, I think I’ve got a new idea for dinner tonight.      Oh? What’s that?      I found this recipe for a spicy chicken and sweet potato casserole. It’s supposed to be really good. I think it’s from a blog I follow.      That sounds nice. I’ve been wanting to try something different. Maybe we can even do it together?      That’d be great. I’d rather cook with you than try to do it alone. I’ve had enough of burnt everything.      Speaking of burnt things, have you tried that new wine from the shop? I think it’s called “Harvest Moon.”      No, I haven’t. I’m not really into wine, but I suppose it’s worth a try. I mean, it’s not like I have much else to do these days.      I actually had a bottle last night. It was really good. I think it’s a Pinot Noir. It had this earthy flavor with a hint of berries.      Hmm, sounds interesting. I might try that. I’ve been meaning to get back into wine. It’s just been too long since I had a proper bottle.      I could bring a bottle over if you want. I’ve got a few from the last supermarket sale. They’re all different, but I think they’re decent.      That’d be great. I’d love to taste some. Maybe we can even have a little game night after. I’ve got a few board games I’ve been wanting to play.      That’d be awesome! I’ve got a new board game I just bought. It’s called “Catan.” It’s a strategy game. You build settlements and trade resources.      Sounds fun. I’ve heard of it. I think I could handle it. I mean, I’ve played a few strategy games before.      Alright, then. Let’s plan on having a night in with some good food, wine, and games.

So, I just got an email about the TEFL conference in Manchester next month. You know, the one that’s supposed to be really big. I’m thinking of going, but I’m not sure if I can afford it.      Oh, you should go! It’s a great opportunity to network and learn new teaching methods. I was there last year and it was amazing. The workshops on differentiated instruction were especially useful.      I’ve heard about that. It’s just the cost is a bit high. I mean, flights, accommodation, and the registration fee… it adds up. Plus, I’ve got a lot of marking to do before the conference.      I get that, but you have to invest in yourself. The conference might just help you get that promotion you’ve been hoping for. I mean, the last time I went, I met a few people who ended up hiring me for part-time teaching roles.      That’s true. I’ve been thinking about expanding my teaching portfolio a bit. Maybe adding some online courses or something. But I feel like I need more skills to do that.      You’re not the only one. I’ve been in the same boat. I actually applied for a grant through the local education board – it’s for teachers who want to attend conferences or take professional development courses. Let me check the details again and send them to you.      That sounds perfect. I should have thought of that earlier. But I’m still not sure about the timing. I have a few school events coming up, and I don’t want to leave my students hanging.      Yeah, it’s about balancing work and personal development. You can’t do one without the other. I understand completely. Maybe we could go together? I know it’d be cheaper if we split the costs.      That’s a good idea. I’d feel more comfortable going if I knew someone else was going. Plus, it would be nice to catch up and share ideas.      Definitely. We can talk more about it this weekend. I’ll bring the grant details and we can plan our schedules. And don’t worry, I’ll help you with the marking while you’re away.      You’re a lifesaver. I owe you one. I’ll be in touch later this week with what I think.      No problem. Just remember, you’re not alone in this.

So, I just wanted to say, I think I’ve found a great spot for parking near the side of the road. It’s not too far from the next village, and it’s got decent lighting. I was worried we might have to drive all the way into Rzeszow just to find a place to park, but now I think we’re good.      That's great, I'm glad you found something. I was just thinking about how much I miss parking in a proper car park, not just some random spot by the side of the road. But honestly, it's kind of fun, you know? It makes the journey feel more like an adventure.      I suppose it does. Though I'm starting to get a bit tired. I think I’ll take a short walk to the village and grab some coffee. It’s been a long drive from Tarnow, and I feel like I need a break.      That sounds like a plan. But don’t be too long—our campervan’s got a bit of a knack for getting stuck in the mud if we leave it too long. I’ve seen it happen before.      Haha, I’ll be careful. I’ve been thinking about how much I used to love reading. I mean, before all this travel, I was always devouring books, especially ones about history and travel. I think I picked up a few books in Tarnow, some Polish ones, actually.      Oh, that sounds interesting. I’m more of a fiction person, to be honest. I tend to read crime or romance novels when I can. But I do enjoy a good historical account too. Did you pick up any about Poland?      I did. One of them was about the 19th century. It was written in Polish, but I have a bit of a grasp of the language, so I managed to get through it. Though I had to look up a lot of words. I think I mentioned before that I once used to teach English, right?      Yeah, you did. You said you were a part-time TEFL teacher. It’s funny—now I’m doing the same thing, but in a different way. I’m a full-time English as a Foreign Language teacher, but I often volunteer with a local community center, teaching kids in the evenings.      That’s amazing. I always thought volunteering could be a good way to stay active and meet people.

You know, I was just thinking about how much the world has changed since I was a kid. I mean, back then, people didn’t talk about things like telomeres or anti-aging treatments the way we do now. It’s crazy how much we’ve learned about the body and how we can slow down the aging process.      I agree. I remember reading that some scientists believe telomeres are like the “biological clock” of cells. When they get shorter, the cell ages. But I don’t know if that’s true. It all sounds so complicated. I mean, I’m more interested in things like global warming and comets. My toddler keeps asking me about the stars and why the sky is blue. I’m not sure I can explain it properly.      You’ve got to be patient. Kids are curious about everything. I remember when I was little, I used to be fascinated by the Vikings, you know? I’d read all these stories about them sailing across the sea and conquering new lands. It’s funny how history impacts our understanding of the world today.      Yeah, I think history is one of those things that people often take for granted. My brother used to talk about how the pyramids were built, and I was always amazed. Now I wonder if they even knew about tectonics back then. It’s like we’ve unlocked so many secrets about the Earth, but we still have so much more to learn.      I guess that’s the thing with life. There’s always more to discover, whether it’s in science, history, or even the way we live our days. I’ve been thinking about taking a weekend away. Maybe we could go kayaking somewhere near the coast. It’s been a while since we had a proper break.      That sounds nice. I’ve been meaning to get out of the house. I’ve been stuck with the toddler for weeks, and I’m starting to feel like I’ve lost my own identity. Maybe we could plan a trip to the mountains? I’ve heard that’s a good place for recharging.      Yeah, I could use a break too. I’ve been working so much lately that I don’t even have time to think about what I want. It’s all about planning, risk, and how we manage our time.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that time we tried that new Italian restaurant in the village? The pasta was so spicy, I thought I was going to cry.      Oh, I remember! You were like a tomato in a saucepan—red, bubbly, and full of drama. But honestly, it was a good place. I still go there sometimes when I want to feel fancy.      Yeah, and you forgot to order the bread. Didn’t even look at the menu. You just said, “Whatever, I’m just here for the wine.”      My bad. I was too distracted by the ambiance. It was like a scene from a movie. But seriously, I was thinking about getting a coffee maker. It’s been ages since we’ve had fresh coffee at home.      That sounds like a good idea. I’ve been ordering takeaway coffee every day, and it’s getting expensive. I was just thinking about using some of the vouchers we got from the supermarket.      Yeah, those vouchers are a godsend. I’ve been saving up for a new baby chair for the nursery. You know, the one with the removable wipes and everything.      Oh, I saw one online the other day! It’s this cute blue one with a little cartoon chicken. I thought it was a bit too childish, but then I thought maybe it’d be nice for the baby to have something fun.      A chicken? I’m not sure about that. I still remember the time you tried to name your pet parrot “Sir Cluck.”      That was a  masterpiece ! I still laugh every time I think about it. But seriously, the chicken is a great idea. I think it’s better than the generic ones.      Speaking of chickens, I was thinking about getting a couple of chickens for the garden. We’ve had that fruit tree for ages now, and it’s started to bear fruit.      Oh, really? You’re going to start a chicken farm? I mean, I’m not sure about your skills with that. I’ve heard you once tried to build a birdhouse out of a shoebox.      That was a  masterpiece ! It ended up looking like something from a science experiment.      Okay, okay, I’ll admit it. But I think it’s time we finally got some chickens. They’ll be good for the garden, and I can finally make some home-grown eggs.

You know, I was just thinking about how different things were when I was your age. I remember putting up the Christmas tree every year, and it was always such a big deal. I used to get so excited, even though I was just a kid.      Yeah, I remember you telling me about that! But I guess it’s not the same now, right? I just put the tree up, and then it’s gone by January. It’s not as much of a big deal. But I do love the feeling of the tree being up. It’s like the whole house comes alive.      That’s true. And you know, I still get that same excitement every year. It’s just that I’m not the one putting it up anymore. I think it’s funny how even though I’m older, I still feel like I’m part of the tradition.      And you’re not the only one who’s still into the tree. My boyfriend, Sam, actually got really into it this year. He even got a new one that’s taller than the one from last year. It’s like he’s trying to outdo himself.      How lovely – but I hope it doesn’t end up falling over again. I remember last year, he nearly knocked it down when he was trying to get the lights on.      Oh, he was so embarrassed. But he didn’t give up. He just kept at it until it was all up. It was like watching a little kid trying to build a house.      That’s the spirit. But talking about decorations, I was just thinking about what you said the other day about your new tattoo. It’s a German design, isn’t it?      Yeah, it’s based on a traditional German folk design. I told you I was going to get it for my birthday. You were the first one to say it was a good idea.      I’m glad I was there to encourage you. You know, I did a bit of German history at university, so I can tell you that their traditions are pretty rich. Just don’t expect to see elves in the Christmas market. That’s more of an English tradition, really.      Oh, I know. But I still think it’s cool. I mean, it’s not every day you get to wear a traditional German outfit and enjoy a homemade bratwurst.

So, I’m officially in my new flat in Sussex. It’s a bit of a shock after living in Bedford for so long, but I’m really excited. The view from the window is amazing, and the flat is much bigger than I expected.      That’s great to hear! I’m glad you like it. I can’t wait to see it myself. But I’ve got to ask—how’s the internet? I know you had a lot of trouble with your last place.      Oh, it was a nightmare. I had to call the provider three times just to get a basic connection. But I think things are better here. The landlord said they’ve already installed the cables and everything. My friend from uni said they’ve got a good provider in this area. I’m going to test it tomorrow, though. I don’t want to end up with zero signal again.      That would be a disaster. I’m actually trying to get my own flat soon, so I’m watching everything closely. I’ve been thinking about what to buy first. I need a fridge, a cooker, maybe a washing machine. I don’t want to overcrowd the space, though.      Yeah, I had to buy a lot of stuff from the local market. I got a few things second-hand, which saved me money. You should check out the local shops. The butcher there sells really fresh meat, and the vegetable seller has some amazing seasonal produce. There’s also this little café near the train station that serves great coffee.      That sounds lovely. I’d love to go there. I’ve been trying to cook more lately, but I’m not very good at it. I’m thinking about joining a cooking class. Do you know anyone who recommends one?      I know a few people who have taken classes. Maybe I can ask them for recommendations. Oh, and by the way, I noticed the nursery next door. The kids are super loud, but I think it’s normal. I hope it doesn’t get too disruptive.      That’s true. I always thought nurseries were a little too noisy, but I guess it’s part of the neighborhood. I’ve also been trying to figure out the rubbish collection schedule. I don’t want to miss any bins or get fined.      You’ll be fine. I had to call the local council to get the schedule.

So, how’s life treating you since you moved back from India? I know you’ve been working on that graduate placement, right?      It’s been interesting. I’ve been settling in pretty well, actually. The job’s not the most exciting, but it’s steady. I’ve been trying to make the most of it, even though it feels like I’m just waiting for something better to come along.      Fair enough. I can relate to that. I’m still in the same place, working as a project co-ordinator for a small firm. It’s not the most glamorous role, but it gives me enough flexibility to do what I love on the side. Still, I’ve been thinking about my future a lot lately. Maybe I should consider moving back to London or somewhere closer to family?      That’s a big decision. But if you’re thinking about it, you should definitely do it. I mean, I know it’s a bit of a leap, but you’ve always been the adventurous type. You’d be so much more comfortable in a bigger city—especially with your graduate degree.      Yeah, I guess. But it’s not just about the location. It’s also about what I want to do with my career. I’ve been thinking about pursuing a master’s program. Maybe in digital marketing or something related to my current role. I just need to figure out how to fund it and whether it’s worth the time and effort.      That sounds like a solid plan. If you’re serious about it, maybe we can help each other out with the application process. I mean, I’m still figuring things out myself, but I’d be happy to support you in any way I can. We’re friends, right?      Of course! I’d love that. It would be nice to have someone to bounce ideas off of. Speaking of which, how are your holidays going? You said you were going to visit your parents in India next month. Any plans for that?      Yeah, I’m going back in a couple of weeks. It’ll be my first time going back since the pandemic, so I’m really looking forward to it. I want to catch up with the whole family and maybe even visit some places I didn’t get to see before. It’s going to be a bit of a cultural shock, but I’m ready for it.

So, I was just telling my mates how I was in the North East when I was younger and I thought I was so cool with my flannel shirts and Doc Martens. Now I'm in Cambridge, and I look like I've been through a washing machine.      I can relate. I grew up in Birmingham, and I used to think I was the epitome of style with my baggy jeans and band T-shirts. But now, I just wear the same old hoodie and jeans every day. It's the PhD life, mate.      Yeah, I get it. But I can't help but miss the real vibe of the North East. You know, the gritty streets, the late-night gigs at The Castle, and the way everyone knows your name. It’s a place where you can't just walk in and be invisible.      I envy you that. I've been to Newcastle a few times, and it’s got that real character. I remember seeing a gig at the Castle once. It was one of those nights where the whole place was packed, and the place was vibrating with energy. Like, you could feel the music in your bones.      Oh, I remember that! I was there with my mates, and we somehow got tickets to see a band I'd never heard of before. Turns out, they were amazing. I still have the T-shirt from that night. It’s like a badge of honor.      That’s the spirit! I think that's what makes the North East so special—people are genuine, and they have this real sense of community. You don't get that in the city, do you? It's all about the scene, the music, the bars, the people.      Exactly. And that's why I've always felt more at home in the North East than anywhere else. I mean, I was born there, and even though I'm now in Cambridge, I can't shake that part of me. I still keep in touch with my old mates, and we talk about how things have changed. It's always interesting.      I hear you. I think there's something about growing up in a place like that that shapes you. You go through all those years of school, of parties, of first loves, and you build this deep connection to your roots. Even if you end up in a completely different part of the country, you still carry that with you.

Grandpa, I brought some crisps and a chocolate bar. You're gonna love this stuff. It's all from the shop in town.      Oh, you're a lifesaver, love. I’ve been craving a treat all day. But what about the news? Have you heard anything about the new council proposals? I heard they're talking about closing the local library again.      Yeah, I saw something about that on the news last night. I don’t get it—how can they afford to build new sports centers but not keep the library open? It’s a bit strange, isn’t it?      It is, and it's not just the library. I mean, the town’s been going through a lot of changes, hasn’t it? I remember when we had a community center and a post office and a butcher’s shop all on the same street. Now it’s just a few shops and a few places that don’t even stay open after five.      It’s so different from when I was growing up here. I used to walk to the library all the time. It was just across the road, and I’d read comics and watch the ducks in the pond. But now, I don’t even know where the library is. I think it’s been moved to a bigger building out by the motorway.      I know. I tried to go the other day, but the building was being renovated. They said it’d be done by the end of the year. I’m worried about the kids. If the library’s gone, what do they do? There’s not much else for them to do in the town. I remember when I was your age, we used to go to the park every Friday and play football with the other kids. Now, it feels like something’s missing.      I guess it’s just the way things are changing. I mean, the government’s been cutting back a lot on public services. I heard the mayor’s talking about trying to get more funding, but I don’t know if it’ll help. It’s like the town’s losing its soul.      That’s what I’ve been saying all along. We need to bring people together, you know? Maybe we could start a community group or something. It’s not like we don’t have the passion for it.

So, what do you think about that blood moon last night? I swear it looked like a giant red apple in the sky. It was pretty spooky, wasn’t it?      Yeah, it was kind of weird. I mean, it was beautiful, but I couldn’t help but think about all the old legends. Some people say it’s a sign of something bad happening, right?      Oh, don’t listen to that. My sister-in-law was convinced it was a bad omen, but I told her it was just the Earth’s shadow. I mean, I’ve seen worse things at the park.      Yeah, but you know what’s worse than a blood moon? Not having the chance to see it properly because you’re babysitting your grandkids. I was about to grab my telescope when I got a call saying the kids were playing with a firework.      Aye, I remember when I was your age, we used to chase the moon with sticks and stones. You don’t see that kind of thing anymore. It’s all fancy gadgets and apps now.      You’re right. My gran used to tell me stories about the moon and the stars when I was little. She said they were like old friends watching over us. I miss those stories.      I miss them too. I’ve been trying to read up on constellations, but it’s hard with a toddler around. I can’t even get my head down for more than five minutes.      You’re not the only one. We’ve had our share of late nights and early mornings. But that’s what family’s for, right? Maybe we should do something like that again. Maybe take the kids to Fitzgeralds Park sometime. The views are great there, and it’s not too far from here.      That sounds good! I’ve heard the park has a nice view of the moon. Maybe we can go on a clear night. I’d love to see it with my own eyes.      If you want, I could help. I’ve got a bit of experience with the stars. I’ve been teaching my grandkids a bit too. It’s a shame I can’t really do anything with them now, but I can still share stories.      That would be lovely. I’d like that. It’s so nice to have people around who remember the old ways.

Well, I've been meaning to ask you about that Scottish referendum thing. You know, the independence vote? It was all over the news last week. I heard some of my colleagues were pretty split on it. I don’t think I’d ever have considered it myself, but I can see why some people might want to break away.      Oh, that was a big deal, wasn’t it? I remember the whole country was buzzing about it. I had a few friends who were quite vocal about it. Some were in favor, others were against. Didn’t you hear about the one guy who got into a big argument with his neighbor over it? I think it got to the point where they almost came to blows.      Haha, that’s the sort of thing I’m talking about. I suppose it showed how passionate people can get about it. But I’m not sure I’d have been able to take that kind of stance. I mean, I’m not against the idea of independence, but I think the way it’s been handled has been a bit hasty. I mean, do you think it’s going to change things much?      I don’t know. It might not. I’ve been thinking about it a lot since then. I mean, I’ve got a small business here in Brighton, and I’m worried that if Scotland goes independent, it might affect trade. But then again, maybe it’s better for them to be in control of their own economy. I just hope it doesn’t end up causing more problems than it solves.      I agree. It’s a complex issue. I had a job interview last week, actually. I’ve been looking for a new role since I retired from teaching. I thought I was going to be back in the classroom, but things have changed. I’m trying to find something that keeps me busy, but I’m not sure what. I mean, I still enjoy working with people, but I just don’t know where to start.      That sounds like a lot to handle. I can imagine how hard that must be. I’ve been thinking about my own situation, too. I’m not as old as you, but I’m trying to figure out what comes next. I’ve got a daughter who’s in her early twenties, and I’m trying to get her into a good job.

So, Dad, I was just thinking—when you were younger, did you ever try to cook a meal without burning anything? I mean, I’ve seen you try to make a proper meal once, and it ended up being like a charcoal briquette on the stove.      Oh, I was terrible at it. I think I once tried making a lasagna and ended up with a sauce that looked more like a soup. My mother used to say I was like a chef in a different galaxy—never quite on Earth.      I remember when Aaron tried to cook for us last week. He said he was going to make a stir-fry. By the time he finished, the kitchen smelled like a fire alarm. I had to rescue the noodles from the pan before they turned to ash.      That doesn’t surprise me. I’ve been in enough kitchens to know that cooking is like driving on ice—everyone’s got their own style, but no one’s actually in control.      Yeah, but I think it’s part of the charm. You know, when you’re cooking with someone, it’s like a team-building exercise. Even if it ends in disaster, at least you shared the experience.      Exactly. I think the worst part of cooking is when you’re all alone. There’s no one to blame, no one to share the effort. But when you’re with people, it’s like a group project. You can laugh, you can argue about spices, and sometimes you end up with something decent.      I’ve always thought that cooking is a language in itself. It’s like a form of communication where you don’t speak words, you just cook. And if you do it right, it tells a story.      Well, I’m not sure about the storytelling part. I think I once made a cake that looked like a cake, but tasted like a puddle. I called it  The Great British Melt .      That sounds like a classic. I once made a roast chicken that was so overcooked, it looked like a football. I think I got a few sympathetic looks from the neighbors that day.      You’re not the only one. I remember when I was younger, I tried making a soufflé. It collapsed before it even got to the table. My dad had to pretend to like it so I wouldn’t feel embarrassed.

So, I was thinking, do you know what it would be like if we got to see some proper farm animals up north? I mean, I’ve seen a few cows and pigs in the countryside, but I’ve never seen a sheep farm up close.      You know, I reckon I’ve seen more farm animals than most people. When I was younger, I used to visit my uncle’s farm in the north. It was like a whole world of its own. They had sheep, cows, pigs, and even a few chickens. You could hardly walk five paces without stepping over a fence or something.      Yeah, I guess that’s the thing. It’s just not something you see every day in the city. I mean, I rode past a few farms on the way here, but they were all just fields and a couple of sheds. Not much else.      You’re both missing out. I once went to a farm in the south with my dad—there were cows, horses, ducks, geese, and even a few pigs. It was like walking through a storybook. You could hear them all at once, like a symphony.      Yeah, I’d love to see that. I mean, I did grow up near the coast, so I’ve seen a few sheep on the hills, but nothing like that. I wonder if there are any farms near here that let people visit?      Well, I don’t know about near here, but I can tell you there’s a place called Worsley Farm not far from the town. It’s a mix of cows and sheep, and they do let people come and see the animals. You can even feed them if you want.      That sounds fun. I’d actually like to go there sometime. It’s always nice to get out of the city and see something real. I mean, as an engineer, I’ve seen a lot of machinery and structures, but not much in the way of living things.      That’s a good point. I think it’s something we all need to remember—don’t just focus on work and tech. Sometimes, you need to go back to basics. Like, what’s the point of having all these gadgets if you can’t even tell a cow from a goat?      Exactly. And besides, you never know—maybe you’ll end up falling in love with a sheep.

So, I was just telling my partner about the time I tried to cook a roast dinner and ended up with a burnt chicken and a very confused cat. You know, the one that watched me for 20 minutes before finally walking away in disappointment.      That sounds like a classic family story. I remember when I was younger, I tried to make a soufflé once and it collapsed like a pancake. My mother was so upset, she ended up making her own soufflé and just served it as a joke. But, honestly, I think I’ve learned my lesson—stick to simple meals when I’m cooking for the family.      I still remember my first time cooking for my family. I tried to make a proper Sunday roast, but I burnt the potatoes and undercooked the meat. It was a disaster. My father just said, “Well, at least you tried,” and that was that. But he’s the one who actually hides the burnt food when he thinks no one’s looking.      Oh, I can relate. I think we’ve all had those moments where we tried to be the star of the dinner table and ended up being the star of the mess. But I have to say, I’ve been trying to get better. I’ve joined the local choir, and I think it’s helped me with my rhythm and timing—though not my cooking.      Oh, you're in the choir? That’s great. I’ve been meaning to join one too. It’s a nice way to meet people and get some exercise as well. Do you do any other activities besides singing?      I’m still trying to get back into exercise. I used to play cricket when I was younger, but it’s been a while. I’ve been going for walks with the neighbors, though. It’s a nice way to stay active and chat with people. Plus, it helps me get some fresh air.      That’s a good idea. I’ve been doing a bit of gardening with my daughter. It’s a peaceful way to spend the mornings, and it keeps me moving. I’m also thinking about starting a community garden in the village. It would be a great way to give back and get some of the locals involved.      That sounds like a wonderful idea. Philanthropy is something I’ve always been interested in, especially with my job.

Okay, so I’ve just read through the Parent’s Evening feedback. It’s... quite sobering, honestly.      Mmm? What’s wrong?      Is it about school?      Yeah, it is. The teacher said that both of you are making great progress in English and Science, but... well, Maths is a bit of a struggle.      Is it because I don’t like numbers?      Not exactly. It’s more about the approach. The teacher mentioned that you both get confused with word problems. Like, you know the answer, but you can’t translate the words into the actual calculation.      Like when the question says, “There are 10 apples and you eat 3, how many are left?” And I just stare at it, like, “What’s the point?”      I know! It’s so weird. I thought I was good at Maths. I mean, I can count to 100, right?      You can count to 100, but you don’t know how to apply it. It’s not just about numbers—it’s about understanding the question.      So what do we do?      Well, we’re going to need to work on it more at home. Maybe some practical examples—like using coins or measuring things around the house. Also, I’m going to talk to the teacher about whether they can provide some extra worksheets or one-on-one support.      Can we do it after dinner? I’m not sure I can focus if I’m still hungry.      Of course. We can do it after dinner, or maybe on weekends. Whatever works for you.      Wait… what’s the point of doing Maths anyway?      Hmm. That’s a good question. Maths is about problem-solving, logic, and understanding how the world works. It’s not just about numbers—it’s about thinking.      Like, like when we read books?      Exactly! Just like characters in books, we have to figure out their motivations, their journeys, and how they change. It’s all about understanding the world, whether it’s in a story or in real life.      Like the circus? They have to solve problems before they can ride the trapeze.      Or like when you try to make a cake and you have to measure the ingredients right.      Okay, I get it. So we’re gonna practice more.      Exactly. And if we ever get stuck, we can always ask each other. We’re a team.      Yeah! Team Math!      Team Math!      Good.

You know, I still can’t get over how that kid from the curtain shop—Oisin—talks like he’s got a dictionary stuffed in his pocket. “I’m gonna be a  professional  tennis player,” he says, like he’s already won Wimbledon and got the endorsement deals.      Oh, don’t get me started. I swear, he’s got more words than a thesaurus. The other day, he was trying to explain to his sister why the sky is blue, and he started talking about Rayleigh scattering and the electromagnetic spectrum. I couldn’t even understand half of it.      Yeah, and then he said, “But it’s not just the sun, it’s the atmosphere.” I almost fell off my chair. I mean, he’s only five, for God’s sake! Wait, does he even know what the atmosphere is?      Mmm, nope. I don’t think he does. But he  thinks  he knows, and that’s what’s scary.      You know, I think he just remembers what he heard on YouTube. I remember him watching that video about “how the world works” and then quoting it verbatim like it’s gospel.      Yeah, and the worst part? He uses it as an excuse to not do his homework. “I’m gonna be a scientist, so I can just learn this stuff later.” I don’t even know what to say.      That’s the thing, though. He’s got a brain. That kid’s got a future. Maybe even a Nobel Prize.      Don’t let him hear that. He’ll think he’s already won.      Speaking of future, did you get the invitations for the birthday party? I was thinking we should have it at the rugby match. You know, stick to the kid’s interests. He’s been talking about it nonstop.      Yeah, I saw the email. You’re right, it’s the perfect chance to go out and get some fresh air. It’s been so long since we’ve all gone to a game together. And the kids might even get to meet your cousin’s son. I heard he’s into rugby too.      Oh, he’s more into games than actual sports. But I’ll admit, he does like the roar of the crowd. I think he’s got a crush on the ref.      Well, whether he likes it or not, we’re going. And before that, we need to make sure we’ve got all the arrangements sorted.

So, I was thinking, maybe we could try one of those word games that involve changing one letter at a time to turn one word into another. You know, like "cat" to "dog" or something. It’s the kind of game that makes you think and it’s kinda fun.      Yeah, I’ve done that before. It’s called a ladder, right? I think it's called a “word ladder” or something like that. But I’ve never really gotten into it. I mean, it’s more of a puzzle, and I prefer doing things like logic puzzles or even math problems.      Yeah, but it’s not just about the puzzle. It’s about the creativity. Like, when you’re trying to figure out what word you can change the next letter to, it can be really rewarding. And sometimes you come up with words you didn’t even know existed. I did one last week where I went from “bass” to “bass” and it took me three steps, but I had to go through “bass” to “bass” again. It was a loop. It was ridiculous.      Oh wow, that’s a loop. That’s so meta. I guess it’s like a real-life version of that joke about the chicken crossing the road. You don’t even know what the point is. But I think we could try it. Maybe pick a random word someone says in the conversation and try to turn it into another word.      That could work. Or maybe we can do something like a rhyme scheme or a word chain. You know, where you start with a word and then the next word has to start with the last letter of the previous one. Like “cat” to “tiger” to “rabbit” to “tiger” again. It’s like a little game of musical chairs.      I think I’ve done that with some of my friends. You can get really creative. It’s almost like a conversation where you’re trying to keep the flow going. It can be funny too. Like, if someone says “apple” and then you say “elephant,” then “tiger,” then “rabbit,” and then “tiger” again.      Yeah, I can see that. It can get a bit circular, but I think it’s a good way to keep the mind active. I mean, as a corpus administrator, I deal with a lot of language data, and I think it helps me think about how words relate to each other.

So, remember when we were in that flat in Manchester and we tried to play  The Smiths  at full volume while napping? I swear, half the building thought we were having a fight.      Yeah, I remember you getting up in the middle of the night, screaming “I’M NOT DOING IT ANYMORE!” like it was the end of the world. I think we both ended up waking up the whole floor.      You were the one who started it! You said, “If we don’t play it loud, we’re not really  living .” I was just trying to sleep, okay? It was like a MySpace mixtape gone wrong.      I still have the old mixtape, by the way. It’s in a shoebox in my flat. I sometimes think about how much we’ve changed since then.      Yeah, and I still play  The Smiths  whenever I’m feeling down. It’s like,  there it is , the music that got me through uni. Though I have to say, your taste in music is still pretty weird.      Oh, please. You were the one who tried to teach me about jazz. I still remember you trying to explain  Miles Davis  like it was some kind of spiritual experience.      And you didn’t even understand the lyrics! I mean, someone had to translate  Kind of Blue  for you. It was like we were speaking different languages.      But you were the one who  actually  understood it. You could tell the difference between a trumpet and a sax, and you even had this weird obsession with 70s funk.      I had a phase. Still do, to be honest. I tried to explain it to my flatmate once, and he just looked at me like I was talking in code. He said he liked  Coldplay . I don’t know how he’s still alive.      You were right about one thing—Coldplay’s not going to get you through a breakup. You need something with more grit. Something that actually  feels  like you’re fighting.      Yeah, and I think I found it. That  Stutter  album your mum brought over. It’s like  The Smiths  meets  Kendrick Lamar —it’s got that raw energy I needed after the last argument with my sister.      You’ve been going through a lot lately. I still can’t believe you two ended up in a fight over a sauce. I mean, it was  baked beans !      You’re not even going to pretend you didn’t enjoy that, are you?

So, I just got an email about the council planning committee meeting. They want us to submit an application for the new housing development near the old industrial site. I think we need to be sure we cover all the bases.      Yeah, I saw that too. The council is really pushing for more housing, especially in areas like that. But I worry about the impact on the local community. We need a solid case for why this development is needed and how it will benefit everyone.      Exactly. I was thinking we should start by outlining the demand for housing in the area. The population is growing, and the current housing stock is just not enough. Plus, we need to address the environmental concerns. They want to see our plan for green spaces and sustainable infrastructure.      I agree. I've been looking into some of the studies from the local university. It seems like there’s a real push for mixed-use developments that include shops, parks, and maybe even some community centers. It would create a more sustainable, self-contained neighborhood.      That’s a good point. I think we should also consider the educational angle. If we can show that the development will support local schools and maybe even create jobs, that might help sway the committee.      Definitely. I was also thinking about the structure of our application. Should we have a section dedicated to long-term sustainability, or maybe a part that outlines potential partnerships with local businesses?      That sounds like a great idea. We could also include a timeline for construction and a breakdown of the phases. I think it would make our proposal look more organized and professional.      Right, and we need to make sure we address any potential objections. For example, the noise during construction, the impact on traffic, and the effect on existing residents. We should be proactive with those concerns.      I was also thinking about including some local testimonials. If we can get a few residents to speak up in favor of the development, that might help. We can reach out to some of the community leaders or neighborhood groups.      That’s a good move. It would show that the community is on board. I think we should also consider holding a public meeting or information session to gather more feedback before submitting the formal application.      I like that. It makes the process more transparent and builds trust.
