Alright, lads, let’s talk about something interesting. You know, I was reading this old folk tale the other day, and it got me thinking about good versus evil. You ever hear the one about the witch who lived in the woods?      A witch? Like the one who turned people into animals?      Yeah, that one! My grandpa told me about it. He said the witch was really mean and would steal people’s babies.      That’s the one. But you know what? My book said that the witch wasn’t so bad. She was just lonely, and she wanted to be loved. So, the moral is that even the meanest people can have a reason for their actions.      But isn’t being mean still bad?      That’s a good question. It’s not about being mean, it’s about understanding why someone is being mean. Sometimes, people do bad things because they’re hurting, or they’re scared. It’s not always about being evil.      But what if someone is really evil? Like, they don’t care about anyone?      That’s a tough one. In some stories, there are real villains who are truly evil. But even then, there’s always a reason. Maybe they were hurt before, or they were taught that being bad is the only way to get what they want.      So, are all the bad guys in the stories real people?      Not exactly. Some of them are just exaggerated versions of real people. Like the witch. She was based on a real person who lived in the woods a long time ago. But over time, the story changed, and people added more details.      So, are there good people in the stories too?      Oh, absolutely. There are heroes who do good things, even when it’s hard. They stand up for what’s right, even when others are scared. That’s what makes them heroes.      Like the knight who fought the witch?      Exactly! But even knights can have flaws. They’re not perfect, but they choose to do the right thing. That’s what makes them good.      So, it’s not about being perfect, it’s about choosing to do the right thing?      That’s one way to look at it. And that’s what makes stories so interesting, right? They show us the struggle between good and evil, and how people can change.      I like that. So, if someone is mean, maybe they can change too?

So, I just got a message from the school about ANON’s filming trip. They said they’re going to be filming in some old buildings in the town, and I think they’re going to have to do some interviews with locals. Hmm, seems like a good opportunity for her to get out and make some real connections.      Yeah, I know. I think it’s supposed to be a documentary about the history of the town. I remember her saying she was excited about it. But she mentioned something about her leg hurting again. Is it from the running she’s been doing?      Oh, right, she’s been trying to get back into shape. She said she’s been going to the gym a few times a week, even though she still hasn’t quite got the hang of the running machines. She keeps saying they feel like they’re moving backwards.      I’ve heard her complain about that. Maybe she should try the stationary bikes instead? I mean, she’s not even five yet, and she’s already looking for a way to burn calories. I don’t know how she’s keeping up.      Mmm... I don’t think I’ve ever seen a running machine, let alone tried one. I mean, I can run around the garden, but that’s about it. I don’t know how you even use those things.      Yeah, I don’t get it either. I think I’d just fall over if I tried. I mean, it feels like you have to push yourself against something, but it doesn’t really move. I think I’d rather just run outside.      Exactly! I mean, it’s one thing to run when you have a clear space, but those machines are like the opposite of that. I think ANON might be doing more harm than good with that running thing. She’s got a leg injury, and now she’s trying to do more exercises. It’s like she’s chasing her tail.      She told me she was thinking about getting some protein bars too. You know, to help her muscles recover. I’m not sure if that’s a good idea. I mean, I think she’s got enough energy from the doughnuts she’s been eating.      Oh, go on then, tell me about the doughnuts. I mean, I saw her in the kitchen the other day with a box of them, and I thought she was going to eat the whole thing.

So, I heard you mentioned the Green Party at the boot sale last week? You said they were handing out leaflets and talking about renewable energy. I’m more of a traditionalist, you know. I’ve been teaching for over thirty years and I’ve seen a lot of changes, but some things just don’t sit right with me.      Yeah, I reckon they’re doing their best to get people excited about environmental issues. I mean, it’s a noble cause, but I think they’re missing the point a bit. You can’t just wave a leaflet and expect people to change their habits overnight. I’ve got a small business, you know. I can’t afford to switch to solar panels or anything like that.      I agree. I think the Green Party’s more about ideology than practical solutions. It’s admirable, I suppose, but I’ve seen too many promises that don’t pan out. I still remember when we were kids in Brighton, the town used to be more about the sea and the pubs, not politics. These days, it feels like everything’s about agendas.      You know, I’ve been thinking about that myself. It’s like the whole town’s got this new energy, but it’s not always for the better. I remember when the boot sales were just a way to clear out old stuff and meet people. Now they’re more like markets, with all sorts of people coming in and out. You know what I mean?      Definitely. I was at one last weekend, and it was a real mix of ages and backgrounds. I even ran into a former student of mine. He’s got a job in London now, but he still comes back every few months. I asked him about his work, and he said it’s all about “green initiatives” and sustainability. I almost laughed. I mean, I’ve spent my life teaching English, and I still don’t know if I’ve ever heard that word used properly.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? We’re talking about the same word, but it means different things to different people. I’ve been in business for over twenty years, and I’ve seen the world shift. Some people are going green, others are still stuck in the old ways. I think the key is balance. You can’t throw the baby out with the bathwater.

So, I was at the supermarket the other day, and I saw this guy trying to buy a pasty. He looked like he’d just stepped out of a documentary about Victorian England. You know, the kind where people are all in waistcoats and top hats?      Yeah, I’ve seen that. I think they’re called "pasties" in the North, but in the Midlands, we just call them "pasty sandwiches." It’s interesting how regional dialects can affect even the way we talk about food.      Exactly! I mean, I grew up in Sunderland—pasty is a big deal there, right? My mum used to make the best ones. You know, with the steak and cheese, and that secret filling that you never get in the shops. I think it’s like a cultural thing.      Oh, I see. I’ve never had one from a proper kitchen. I’ve only ever had the ones you buy at the supermarket, and they’re just… not the same. I guess it’s like how you get different styles of beer depending on where you are. Like a real ale versus a lager.      Yeah, exactly. I tried a few different ones from the local market last week, and it was like a whole different world. The taste was so much richer. I reckon the pasty is one of those things that defines the North of England. You know, along with the weather and the football.      Definitely. But I can’t help but think about the politics of it. You know, with all the talk about the North and the South, and how people are trying to bring the regions together. I mean, the pasty is a symbol of a certain culture, isn’t it?      Yeah, it kind of is. I mean, I think it’s interesting how something so simple can carry so much history and identity. I remember my gran told me stories about how the pasty was invented by the miners to keep them warm while they worked down the mines. That’s a real story, isn’t it?      I think it is. Though I’m not sure how much of it is true. But it makes for a good anecdote, doesn’t it? You know, those kinds of stories that people tell to explain why they do things the way they do.      Exactly. I think it’s also about fashion, in a way.

To the chaos of life and the even more chaotic wine. How’s your week been, love?      I’d say it’s been a whirlwind. I was up at 5 this morning, teaching a lecture on postmodernism to a class that’s basically just there because of the deadline. I didn’t even get to finish my breakfast. You?      Oh, I had a bit more of a leisurely start. I spent an hour in the garden trying to convince the cat that the daffodils weren’t a threat. She just stared at me like I was a weirdo. I think she’s finally decided I’m not worth the trouble.      That’s the spirit. I’ve been meaning to pick up that art project I started last year. You know, the one where I tried to paint killer whales. It’s been sitting in my studio collecting dust and asking me why I ever thought that was a good idea.      I remember that. You said you wanted to capture their intelligence and grace, but the result was more like a horror movie. I still can’t look at that painting without thinking of  Jaws .      True. I think I ended up using more red than blue. Maybe I should have gone with the killer whale theme for my next lecture. I could call it  The Psychology of Panic in Marine Life .      That’s not a title— that’s  a thesis. You’d get more attention if you just called it  How Not to Paint a Whale .      I take offense to that. I’ve been practicing my brushstrokes. Speaking of which, have you seen the new episode of  Blue Peter ? They had this segment about squatting and the history of that badge. It was ridiculous. They told us how to tie it around our waist like it was a badge of honor.      Oh, I saw that. I think it was more about nostalgia than anything. My parents still have their  Blue Peter  badges from the 80s. They’re faded, but they’re  very  proud of them. I can’t imagine living without one.      I guess it’s something that’s become part of the cultural fabric. I mean, if you don’t have one, are you even British? Or is that just us?      Probably just us. But hey, at least we have each other and our wine. That’s the real badge of honor.

You know, I was just thinking about those hostels we used to manage back in the day. It’s funny how things change. I mean, we had to deal with all sorts of people, some of them real troublemakers, but others were just looking for a bit of stability.      Oh yes, I remember that. It was a tough job, but it kept us busy. I used to wonder if we were making a real difference, or if it was just another way to keep people from causing more trouble. But then again, some of those folks had nowhere else to go.      I still remember the time we had that one guy who kept trying to sell his “vintage” posters. He was always trying to con us, but he was a bit of a character. I think he was just looking for company.      Yeah, and he used to talk about photography like it was the only thing that mattered. I think he still does. I saw some of his photos the other day—wild, but somehow beautiful.      I bet they were. I tried taking some photos once, but I always ended up with blurry faces and half-exposed pictures. I think I need a better camera, but I don’t know where to start.      You know, I could help you with that. I’ve got a bit of experience with cameras. I used to take photos for the school magazine when I was a teacher. Though I’d say I was more of a science guy than a photographer.      Science? You mean like engineering or something? I used to think science was all about numbers and formulas, but maybe I was wrong.      It’s more than that. It’s about understanding how things work. I used to love that. I remember when I was a kid, my parents ran a small shop. They always said that if you could fix a broken toaster, you could fix anything. It’s a bit like that.      My parents ran an abattoir too. They worked hard all their lives. I always thought that life was about working hard, but now I’m not so sure. It’s not always about the money, is it?      I suppose not. I mean, we had a few friends who ended up in the hospital recently. Some of them were working over time, others just got lucky. It’s a reminder that life can change in an instant.

So, I heard you were in recruitment before you became an associate lecturer. That must have been a different kind of work, right?      Oh, it was a few years ago, actually. I worked in recruitment for a few years before I got into academia. It was a bit of a culture shock, to be honest. I mean, I was used to dealing with candidates, but then I moved into a sector where people were actually trying to learn something. It felt like a big shift.      That sounds interesting. How did you end up in recruitment in the first place? Were you doing that before you went to grad school?      Yeah, I was still in my early twenties when I started. I was working part-time while studying for my masters. I needed some extra income, and a friend of mine was in recruitment. He said he could get me a job, and I didn’t really think much about it at the time. It was all about placement and getting people into the right roles, not really about education or development.      That must have been a different kind of satisfaction. I mean, I’ve always been in education, so I’ve seen how people learn and grow. But in recruitment, it’s more transactional. Still, it must have been a good experience for you.      It was, in a way. I learned a lot about people—what they want, what they’re capable of, and how to communicate effectively. But I also realized that I wanted to be part of something more meaningful. When I finished my masters, I thought, “Maybe I can teach people how to think and learn, instead of just placing them in jobs.”      That makes sense. I’ve had a similar experience. I used to be a teacher in a secondary school, then moved into university teaching. I really enjoy the academic side, even if it can be challenging at times. There’s something about facilitating learning that gives you a sense of purpose.      I totally agree. Speaking of which, I’ve been thinking about the literacy levels in our courses. I just had a meeting with the department head about the students in one of my modules. Some of them are struggling with basic academic writing. It’s like they’ve never been taught how to structure an essay or use proper academic language.      That’s a real issue, isn’t it?

Hey, so I just met this guy at the coffee kiosk, and he asked me what I’m studying. I said, “I’m a student, but I’m not sure what I’m studying yet.” He said, “You’re a  student ? Do you even have a degree?” I laughed and said, “I’ve got a graduate degree in  not  knowing what I want to do.”      Oh, I know that feeling. I just got out of the library and I’m still trying to figure out what I’m doing with my life. My boss at the shop says I’m “too smart” for the job, but I’m still working there.      That’s funny. I’m in the same boat. I’m studying for my master’s, but I’m still not sure if I want to do anything with it. My parents say I should be “practical,” but I just want to read books and drink coffee.      Yeah, I feel like we’re all just waiting for life to hand us a plan. But seriously, I think it’s okay. I mean, I’m from Bradford, and I’ve always been told I was too much of a dreamer. But I wouldn’t trade it for anything.      I can relate. I’m from somewhere in the North, and my family never understood why I didn’t just get a “real job.” But I like being around people who are into stuff like this. Speaking of which, I heard you’re from Bolton?      Yeah, I’m from Bolton. My accent is all over the place now, though. I moved to Salford for uni, and it’s like trying to speak English with a twist.      Hey, you all are talking about accents and stuff. I’m from India, but I’ve been living in England for a few years now. I still speak with my accent, and sometimes people think I’m from somewhere else.      Oh, I’ve had that too. I’m from Bradford, so I have that Northern English twang, but I get confused sometimes if people think I’m from somewhere else.      You know, I’ve noticed that sometimes when people from different places talk, it’s like we’re all speaking the same language, but with different accents. It’s like a puzzle.      Exactly! I think it’s part of what makes us all so interesting. I mean, if we all spoke the same way, we’d be like,  what even is a conversation?

Right, so I was thinking about that thing with the military, you know, when we were talking about our uncles the other day. I can't believe my cousin is actually going to join up. He's like, twenty-two, and he's been saying he wants to be a soldier for years now.      Yeah, I know. My brother-in-law did that a while back. He ended up in the Army, and it was a huge change for him. He wasn't even sure if he wanted to go, but he ended up loving it. Though I have to say, I couldn’t imagine doing that. All the rules, the discipline, the hours.      I get that, but I think it’s different for everyone. My mate who went, he said he used to feel like he was just going through the motions at his old job. And when he joined the Army, he found a purpose. I guess it’s not for everyone, but for some, it’s the only way to feel like they’re contributing something real.      That’s true. Although, I have to say, I’ve heard some horror stories. I mean, the military’s not all good vibes. I heard from someone who was in the Reserves that they were doing drills every weekend, and it was exhausting. And then there’s the whole issue of mental health. I remember reading something about PTSD among soldiers. It’s a real problem, isn’t it?      Absolutely. I think it’s important to have support systems in place. You can’t just sign up and expect to come back the same person. That said, I do think it’s a great way to meet people, build skills, and even travel. I mean, I’ve heard of a lot of soldiers going overseas and coming back with new experiences and stories.      Yeah, that’s for sure. I mean, I’m more of a homebody, but I can see the appeal. Although, I’m not sure I’d ever be able to handle the pressure. Speaking of pressure, have you seen the new film about space? I’ve been dying to watch it, but I keep putting it off because I’m so busy with work.      No, I haven’t. I heard it’s supposed to be really good though. Is it the one with the astronaut who goes mad in space?

So, I just got back from the weekend trip to London. It was wild. I mean, it's always wild, but this time it was even more so. I can't believe how many people from there are suddenly showing up here. It's like the entire city has decided to scatter across the country.      Yeah, I saw that on the train. Everyone was in suits, trying to act like they were from the north or the south. I swear, half of them were just trying to sound posh.      Oh, you're not wrong. I had a guy in my flat the other day who insisted he was "from London, but the real London." He was trying to tell me about the "real" culture, like it's not the same here.      It’s so frustrating. I mean, I get that people move for work, but sometimes it feels like it's just about showing off. And then there's the racism. People from London think they're better than everyone else, like they're the capital of the whole country.      Honestly, I think it's the same in every big city. It’s just the human condition. But it still gets annoying. I mean, I've got friends from Manchester, and they’re just as pretentious as the Londoners.      True, but the thing is, not everyone from London is like that. I mean, my cousin is from there, and she’s just a regular person. But yeah, the ones who come here? It’s like they’re trying to outdo each other.      Exactly. And then there’s the whole dating scene. I’ve been on a few dates with people from London, and it’s like they’re always looking for a "real" person. They don’t like people who are from the provinces, like us.      I’ve heard that. I had a girl once who said she could tell I was from the north just by the way I spoke. It’s like they think we’re all the same.      It’s so frustrating. I mean, I’m from Winchester, and I can’t even say I’m from the South without being judged.      Yeah, it’s about time we stood up for ourselves. I mean, we’re not all the same. We’re not all arrogant or pretentious. We’re just people.      Exactly. I think we need to start talking more about this.

So, you've just got here, right? How did you find the flat? I know it's not exactly the most glamorous place in the world, but it's got character, you know?      It was alright. The journey was a bit of a trek from Brighton, but it was worth it. I mean, the view from the window is amazing. You can see the whole valley. It’s like a postcard.      You know, I’ve seen some interesting things in my time. Back in the day, when I was working, I used to drive up to London every week. It was a bit of a commute, but I always thought, "If only I could live in the countryside!" Now I’m retired, and I’m stuck in London. I’m not sure what I’d do if I had to move back.      You can do it, Dave. You just have to find the right place. I used to live in Harlow and it was quite rough, but I made it work. I had to be careful with the bills, though. I remember once, I forgot to pay the utility bill, and it all went to credit control. It was terrifying.      I know. We’ve been trying to get on top of the bills. I got a job as an English teacher, which helps, but the flat is a bit of a pain. The window cleaning was a nightmare. I don’t know how we’re going to get someone to come in. Maybe we can book it through a service?      Oh, we could. I used to have a friend who worked at a cleaning company. She said they do a really good job. I think she mentioned something about the price being reasonable. I can call her and see if she can recommend someone.      You should also be careful with the plastic bags. I’ve heard they’re not good for the environment. I’ve been trying to cut down on them. But I still use them for groceries. It’s a little hard getting used to.      Yeah, I know. It’s a habit. I’ve tried to switch to reusable bags, but sometimes you just get caught up in the moment. I mean, it's not like I'm using a ton of them every day.      You’re not. But it’s all about the small things. I used to be a care assistant, and I saw how people’s habits could change over time.

So, I just got this really weird message from my dad. He said he got a pop-up on his phone that said, “Your account is suspended unless you pay a fine of £50.” And he didn’t even know what it was about. I mean, it looked like a scam, but he’s pretty tech-savvy. I told him to ignore it and he did. But I’m still worried he might have clicked on it. Do you ever get those?      Yeah, I’ve had that same thing. It was like a fake bank alert. I remember I thought it was my bank, but then I checked my account and everything was fine. I think the real banks only ever send messages through official apps or their website. You know, you don’t get these pop-ups on your phone from them.      I think it’s just a way to get people to click and download malware. I mean, even if you do click, you can’t really trust anything anymore, can you?      Exactly. And the thing is, I’ve told my mum about it, and she’s like, “Oh, I got that too!” Like, it’s like a grief of the digital age. You can’t even walk into a café without someone getting a message like that. It’s just part of life now.      I know, right? And I’ve been trying to switch to using more phone apps for everything. Like, I’m even using a food delivery app now. It’s just easier. But I still can’t get over how bad the food is. Some of the delivery is just... weird.      Oh, I know. I had this chicken curry last week that tasted like it had been left in the fridge for a week. It was like a mission to eat it. I told the app I’d give it two stars, but I just didn’t.      I tell you, I’m starting to think I should just cook more. My mum always said, “If you don’t cook, you’ll end up eating nothing but chips and takeaways.” And she’s not wrong. I’ve been trying to cook more lately—like, proper meals. My flatmate’s a vegetarian, so it’s not the easiest, but I’m getting better.      That’s great! You’re not the only one trying to improve. I’ve been working on my cooking skills too.

Well, I've been thinking about work again this morning. I've been on shift all week and it's starting to get a bit much. I mean, sure, I love helping people, but sometimes it feels like there aren't enough hours in the day.      I can relate. I've been working on some tight deadlines too. My boss is always asking for more, but I think they're just not used to working with someone who's actually got a degree. It’s frustrating, honestly.      You two are lucky. I'm stuck with the same old routine, same old people, and same old stressed-out patients. My manager keeps saying I need to "smile more" and "be more positive." I don't know what they think I'm doing when I'm not smiling – it’s not like I have a choice, is it?      I hear you. I'm not even in the same building as my manager, but I still feel like I'm under constant scrutiny. Last week, one of the residents started shouting at me, and I just wanted to tell them to knock it off, but I ended up apologizing for  myself . It’s so exhausting.      I know what you mean. It’s not just the patients; it’s the staff too. I have this colleague who always seems so calm, but I caught her crying in the staff room the other day. I asked her why she wasn’t just taking a break or something, and she said, “I can’t afford to be sick.” That really hit me.      I’m sure that’s not the only story. I had a friend who had to leave her job because of stress. She couldn’t handle it anymore and just walked out one day. I feel bad for her, but I also feel like I can’t do that. My parents have been stressing about my future for years, and I don’t want to let them down.      I know what that’s like. My family always wanted me to be a teacher or something "more stable," but I just wanted to be a care assistant. They never understood the work, even though they’ve seen me work with my mum. She’s got dementia, and I spend more time with her than I do with my own family.      It’s tough, isn’t it?
